text:
With help from Zia Weise in Belgium, Charlie Cooper and Abby Wallace in the United Kingdom, Mike Blanchfield in Canada, Nicolas Camut in France, Benjamin Storrow, Sara Schonhardt and Zack Colman in the U.S., and Brian Dabbs in Singapore.

Surge Preview

How the victory by Germany’s AfD highlights Trump-like energy policies.

A sunken oil tanker in the Middle East pushes crude prices up.

Canada under Carney releases a climate report without fanfare.

A Russian-designed nuclear plant in Hungary is delayed and under review.

BROWN POWER: More coal, more Russian gas, fewer wind turbines: What the rising far right intends for Germany’s energy supply would demolish the country’s much-vaunted Energiewende, the transition from fossil to renewable electricity.

After winning a weekend election in Germany, the Alternative for Germany, or AfD, which rejects the scientific consensus of man-made climate change, may soon get a chance to put some of those plans into action — serving as a bellwether for the fallout of the global disruption to the political establishment on the energy transition.

The AfD on Sunday swept to victory in regional elections in the eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt with 44 percent of the vote. They now have a shot at governing the state, the first time a far-right party would hold power in Germany since the end of World War II. (The AfD’s chapter in Saxony-Anhalt has been labeled as a confirmed extremist organization by the state’s domestic intelligence service, a label the AfD disputes.)

Echoes of Trump: With the party leading in national polls too, the success confronts Germany not only with the question of what lessons have been learned from the Nazi era but also whether the country is ready for an energy policy that mirrors U.S. President Donald Trump’s, and exceeds the plans of other European far-right parties in its radicalism.

Affordability was a front-and-center topic in the Saxony-Anhalt election campaign, alongside concerns about immigration. German energy prices have skyrocketed in recent years, after Russia in 2022 halted the flow of cheap oil and gas for the country’s heavy industrial base, and the war in Iran put further pressure on bills.

The AfD squarely blames the high prices on the Energiewende, a 20-year-old plan to wean the country off both fossil and nuclear power and switch to renewables in a bid to reach net-zero by 2045.

In fact, Germany’s energy prices are high mostly because of a combination of mounting costs for the build-out and modernization of the country’s outdated grid, substantial energy taxes and the expense of fossil fuel generation and imports.

Pleasing Putin: The AfD wants a moratorium for all onshore wind and many solar projects; to end state subsidies for renewables and clean tech such as electric vehicles and heat pumps; to stop Germany’s coal phase-out, scheduled for 2038; to kill all carbon pricing schemes; and to restart the import of Russian oil and gas.

There’s no need for an energy transition in the AfD’s eyes. The party does not believe in man-made climate change, describing it as a “globalist” ideology advocating for a culture of “religious prohibitions” on energy use by consumers and the industry. It wants Germany to leave the Paris climate accord and end all efforts to address global warming.

That’s intentionally similar to the political narrative in Washington. The AfD has modeled its programmatic and populist approach after MAGA, even though the party’s relationship with Trump has been somewhat rocky as of late.

The AfD’s energy and climate playbook does, however, set it apart from its fellow European far-right parties.

Alt party, not alt energy: In all major European countries, far-right groups are attacking renewables and climate policy. But not all champion fossil fuels — the National Rally party of France’s Marine Le Pen, for example, is advocating for more hydropower and nuclear even as it bashes wind turbines — and few bar the AfD deny the reality of climate change.

Poland’s right-wing Law and Justice party has come the closest, recently introducing an anti-green bill that claimed atmospheric CO2 levels were too low and that humans have no influence on the climate. Individual figures in the United Kingdom’s Reform and Spain’s Vox have also questioned the consensus on man-made global warming, but the parties as a whole don’t subscribe to that position. France’s National Rally and Giorgia Meloni’s Brothers of Italy advocate for “pragmatic” green policies.

The AfD, however, is explicit. “Climate change has always existed… The question of the extent to which humans contribute to it remains scientifically unresolved. A so-called Energiewende costing thousands of billions of euros cannot be based on this,” its 2025 manifesto read.

If the party forms the government in Saxony-Anhalt, Sunday’s victory doesn’t hand the AfD the power to change federal energy policy, which is constrained by European and even constitutional law. But a far-right government could slow the region’s renewable energy rollout by obstructing permitting — as well as gaining the platform to build political opposition to the energy transition on a wider scale.

Germany’s next regional election takes place on Sept. 20 in the north-eastern state of Mecklenburg-Vorpommern. The polls once again project an AfD win.

WELCOME TO SURGE: This is Josh Groeneveld, POLITICO’s editor for energy and climate policy in Berlin, where my team and I work hard to make sense of Germany’s quizzical energy policy of phasing out coal in the short term, betting on gas in the medium term and going 100 percent green in the long term. When I’m not doing that, I’m raising two daughters, in the (equally quizzical) hope that they can simply rely on an abundance of fusion energy when they’re older. Send tips, feedback and fusion reactor plans to jgroeneveld@politico.eu.

Driving the (global!) day

TANKER WAR: Oil prices are climbing once again after a new escalation in the Middle East.

U.S. forces on Saturday struck three Iran-linked oil tankers — sinking one — after Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps fired ballistic missiles at two American warships. Iranian state media made unverified claims of retaliatory attacks against six warships.

The Brent crude benchmark price, which has been climbing since late August, rose above $97 per barrel on Monday, its highest since July. “Every escalation, every attack, raises the risk of higher oil prices,” said Ajay Parmar, director of oil markets at ICIS.

Oil has been highly volatile since the U.S. and Israel commenced strikes on Iran in February, with consumers around the world taking the hit through higher prices at the pump.

Between six to eight million barrels per day are passing through the Strait of Hormuz, Parmar said, “far lower than levels pre-war, but generally higher than many may have expected at this point.”

The effect of one incident might be small, he said, but “continued flare-ups” would mean “insurers and shipping operators would likely reduce flows” — sending prices higher still. — Charlie Cooper

HUNGARY’S RUSSIAN PROBLEM: A Russian-designed nuclear power plant being built in Hungary that would be the country’s biggest source of electricity will miss its completion date by at least two years, our colleague Ben Makuch exclusively reports, based on internal documents.

Inside scoop: The spreadsheet was shared by an intelligence official and comes from inside Russia’s state-nuclear corporation, Rosatom. The document contains thousands of cells detailing construction schedules going back as far as 2015 — barely a year after former Hungarian Prime Minister Viktor Orbán and Russian President Vladimir Putin agreed to the Paks II expansion.

Why it matters: Paks II is critical to the future of Hungary’s energy supply. It expands the Soviet-era Paks nuclear plant that already provides nearly half of the country’s electricity but which is currently due to be decommissioned between 2032 and 2037. The two new Rosatom reactors would more than replace that lost power, generating 2400 megawatts. But with estimated costs surpassing €12.5 billion, the expansion is under review by Hungary’s newly elected Prime Minister Péter Magyar for both its price tag and connections to Putin.

BRUSSELS AND BEIJING: Brussels is gearing up for a fight to try and break China’s dominance of cheap solar production. Over the last two decades, as demand for renewable energy generation has soared in Europe, cheap Chinese manufacturers have driven down solar panel prices, leaving domestic clean energy producers on the continent struggling to compete. Factories have been shuttered, expansion plans shelved, and supply chains moved to China. Now, the European Commission wants to use one of its most powerful tools — public spending — to help rebuild Europe’s clean tech industries.

Terms and conditions: Proposed reforms to EU procurement rules, set to drop Sept. 9, could require public authorities to consider factors such as sustainability, supply chain resilience and European production — rather than choosing suppliers primarily on price. Some of those local suppliers, though, fear the overhaul by policymakers is coming too late. “It’s now, not in three years — we have too many companies in Europe that are on the verge of collapse,” said Frederic Conrads, a managing partner at Belga Solar, Belgium’s last solar panel manufacturer. Read more from Aude van den Hove.

Power Players

QUIET ON CLIMATE: With no discernible fanfare, Prime Minister Mark Carney released Canada’s Changing Climate Report 2026 as the country headed into last week’s long holiday weekend.

In character: The potential environmental damage wrought as countries race to meet growing electricity demand in the years ahead is in the minds of policymakers. Carney, formerly the United Nations special envoy for climate action and finance, has faced criticism for rolling back the climate change policies of his predecessor Justin Trudeau.

Burying the lede: Thursday’s report offers 15 “headline statements” summarizing how climate change has and will affect Canada.

Headline No. 5 reads: “In the near term, annual average temperature in Canada is expected to rise by about 1°C from 2021 to 2040.”

This is buried under headline No. 4: “The changes include more extreme heat, less extreme cold, longer growing seasons, longer fire seasons, earlier peak stream flow, shorter snow and ice cover seasons, thinning glaciers, thawing permafrost, warming oceans and rising sea level. Human-caused warming is the only explanation for the collective changes observed.”

Headline No. 9 makes its point more crisply: “Droughts and flash floods will become more frequent and severe with additional warming.”

Lowering the temperature: The lack of fanfare was noticeable, said Ryan Ness, the Canadian Climate Institute’s adaptation research director. When the report was last published in 2019, the rollout included “having ministers do press conferences and having events to explain the contents of the report to Canadians. That approach is certainly warranted here again.”

Hello minister: The office of Environment and Climate Change Minister Julie Dabrusin emphasized Friday the government’s commitment to fight climate change “by taking a pragmatic and durable approach. This includes building major clean energy projects across the country, driving mass electrification, and making significant investment in the low-carbon economy.” — Mike Blanchfield

ELECTRICITY BILLS PLEDGE: Nigel Farage’s deputy at Reform UK, Richard Tice, says he will quit if he does not deliver his pledge to cut Brits’ energy bills by £250 within 100 days, should he end up in government. Tice told Reform’s annual conference it was proof he was “prepared to put my money where my mouth is.” — Abby Wallace

Our open tabs

OUT FRONT: From coal to batteries and renewables: Le Monde writes (in French) how the mining town of Collie in Australia aspires to be a model of successful energy transition.

OPEN THE GATES: Terrapower, the Bill Gates-backed nuclear developer, hopes its U.K. plant will be generating electricity by 2034, the firm told Reuters Monday.

That’s all for today. Thanks for reading!

title: Critical minerals drive US energy security strategy
description:

text:
Rising electricity demand, technological advances and efforts to rebuild US manufacturing are increasing the strategic importance of critical minerals, prompting Washington to secure supplies vital to the economy, defense and advanced technologies.

Strategic raw materials and rare earth elements, a group of 17 elements with specialized properties, play an important role in national strategies.

Critical minerals such as copper, lithium and graphite are essential to the energy transition, defense industries and artificial intelligence technologies.

However, much of the processing and refining of these materials takes place outside the US, leaving the country vulnerable to global supply-chain disruptions.

US President Donald Trump views critical minerals not simply as an economic raw material issue, but as a matter of national security, defense and reducing strategic dependence on China.

China's dominant position in global critical mineral and rare earth supply chains has accelerated bipartisan efforts in the US to strengthen supply-chain security and resilience.

When declaring a national energy emergency after taking office last year, Trump said the US' capacity in energy and critical minerals production, processing, refining and infrastructure was "woefully inadequate" to meet the country's needs.

He linked critical minerals to energy security, manufacturing, transportation, agriculture and national defense.

The administration is seeking to rebuild critical mineral supply chains in the US, from mining and processing to recycling, with the goal of securing the materials needed by strategic industries ranging from defense to artificial intelligence.

- Trump seeks strategic partnerships on rare earth elements

The Trump administration is pursuing an increasingly active international strategy on critical minerals and rare earth elements, seeking to reduce China's dominance by developing alternative sources of supply and strengthening partnerships with allies and strategic partners.

Trump has repeatedly highlighted Ukraine's mineral resources as part of this strategy.

In discussing US financial support for Ukraine, he said he wanted an agreement that would provide the US with access to the country's rare earth elements and other mineral resources.

The US-Ukraine agreement gives Washington an economic interest in and strategic access to future natural resource projects in Ukraine, covering a broad range of underground resources rather than only rare earth elements.

- US moves to strengthen critical minerals infrastructure

The Trump administration has also sought to expand domestic access to critical mineral deposits.

It moved to revive the Ambler Road project in Alaska, linking the project to national security, economic growth and efforts to reduce dependence on foreign sources of strategic minerals.

Trump has also highlighted cooperation with Australia on critical minerals and rare earth elements.

His administration has also pursued broader geopolitical initiatives, including Trump's calls for US ownership of Greenland, which he has primarily framed as a national security issue.

In February, Trump announced the creation of the first Strategic Critical Minerals Reserve, describing it as a stockpile of critical minerals that could be used for civilian purposes during emergencies.

Trump has also directed federal agencies to prioritize US-sourced critical minerals and other strategic materials. In a post on Truth Social, he wrote: "All Federal Agencies Must Buy American - No Excuses!"

Beyond domestic measures, Trump has pushed the idea of establishing a critical minerals trading bloc among Western countries to counter China's influence over global prices and supply. The initiative focuses on minerals including lithium, cobalt, rare earth elements, antimony, graphite and tungsten.

- Washington builds broader network of mineral partnerships

Trump has signed an executive order declaring critical minerals and recyclable critical materials necessary for US national defense and giving the Commerce Department authority to restrict exports of such materials when deemed necessary.

The administration has also announced $3 billion in investments in critical mineral and battery projects.

Washington is also building a network of multilateral and bilateral partnerships aimed at diversifying supplies and challenging China's dominance of global critical mineral and rare earth supply chains.

The US has launched the "Pax Silica" coalition with allies and strategic partners including Australia, Japan, South Korea, Singapore and Israel, aiming to strengthen cooperation around critical minerals, advanced technologies and resilient supply chains.

The White House is also adapting its "America First" approach to raw materials diplomacy by using US financial power to secure critical mineral supplies through a series of bilateral agreements.

These partnerships extend from Southeast Asia to Saudi Arabia and cover a broad range of activities, from mining and mineral processing to the production of magnets and other downstream materials.

By combining US mining and processing capacity with international partnerships and financing from institutions including the Export-Import Bank of the United States (EXIM) and the US International Development Finance Corporation (DFC), Washington is seeking to build a globally diversified mineral supply network.

By Gulsen Cagatay

title: 11 politicians who have changed their tune on data centers - Business Insider
description:
Josh Shapiro, a Democrat, unveiled what he's called "the strictest guardrails in the nation" for future data center development.
When Amazon announced plans to spend $20 billion on data centers, Shapiro touted the "largest private sector investment in the history of Pennsylvania."
"As Illinois grows its status as a technology hub of the future, this data center is bringing investment and vitality to a newly thriving community," Pritzker said in a statement when the data center opened in 2023.
The explanation: A spokesperson for Pritzker said the conversation around data centers has changed with the advent of AI hyperscalers.
His requirements include providing free electricity for homeowners in communities with data centers, requiring data centers to pay full property taxes and then using the revenue to cut Ohio homeowners' property taxes, and requiring the facilities to comply with environmental standards.
text:
In July, Gov. Kathy Hochul, a Democrat, made New York the first state to impose a one-year moratorium on what she called "hyperscale AI data centers."

The details: Her executive order states that the temporary ban applies to data centers that need 50 megawatts or more to operate. Additionally, Hochul separately ordered that data centers either pay for their own power generation or pay more for the energy they need.

Past views: In May, Hochul questioned the need for a more stringent moratorium, which was being considered by the state legislature.

"This is a local decision for municipalities, it's land use, which is the purview of local governments," she told reporters, per E&E News. "It's not a statewide approach necessarily, but it's something I'm looking at intensely."

The explanation: Hochul previously told NBC News that local communities had asked for her assistance.

"At first I thought this is more of a local decision, but then I realized they don't have the negotiating ability, the clout, the wherewithal to be able to negotiate the best benefits or to make sure that these companies, as I said in my State of the State, are either bringing their own power or paying a premium into the grid to cover the cost," she said.

In August, Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro, a Democrat, unveiled what he's called "the strictest guardrails in the nation" for future data center development.

The details: Shapiro's order, which is not a moratorium, requires developers to secure local approval before they can receive state permits, granting more power to communities that Shapiro said have been treated unfairly by some developers. Shapiro also removed data centers from fast-track permitting and established guidelines, including power generation and transparency requirements, that, if developers agree to follow, allow for permit review on a rolling basis, Spotlight PA reported.

"I've heard loud and clear from the good people of Pennsylvania as I've traveled our commonwealth, and I'm here to say today that we will not be bullied by these developers," Shapiro said.

Past views: Shapiro once openly courted data center development. When Amazon announced plans to spend $20 billion on data centers, Shapiro touted the "largest private sector investment in the history of Pennsylvania."

"With this historic announcement, we're creating opportunity for our workers, generating new revenue for our local communities, and ensuring the future of AI runs right through Pennsylvania," he said in a statement released by his office.

The explanation: When asked "what prompted his 180," Shapiro told CBS News, "Look, I listened. I think it's important for elected leaders to actually get the vibes of a community, to listen and to be able to be flexible, to be able to work with a neighborhood."

Arizona Gov. Katie Hobbs, a Democrat, pushed state lawmakers to eliminate a tax incentive for data center development that she called "a thirty-eight million dollar corporate handout."

The details: Ultimately, Hobbs and state lawmakers agreed to a three-year pause on new data center sales tax breaks.

Past views: In calling for the change, Hobbs was open about how, as a state lawmaker, she voted to create the incentive.

"More than a decade ago, we made a strategic decision to grow data centers by creating a tax exemption for them — I voted for it," she said in her State of the State address in January. "Now, Arizona is a national leader in this sector. We must ask ourselves: should taxpayers continue subsidizing the data center industry?"

The explanation: Hobbs said the incentive had boosted the industry, and now it was time for it to stand on its own.

In June, Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker, a Democrat, moved to suspend new tax incentives for data centers.

The details: Pritzker also called on the state legislature to help him advance reforms to data center development that would ensure developers pay their fair share for power use, minimize water use, and be more transparent.

Past views: Pritzker celebrated when his state reeled in major projects, such as Meta's $1 billion data center in DeKalb.

"As Illinois grows its status as a technology hub of the future, this data center is bringing investment and vitality to a newly thriving community," Pritzker said in a statement when the data center opened in 2023.

The explanation: A spokesperson for Pritzker said the conversation around data centers has changed with the advent of AI hyperscalers.

"Responsible governance means reassessing incentives when circumstances change," the spokesperson said. "He supports responsible growth of the industry, but not at the expense of higher utility bills, grid reliability or Illinois' water resources."

Maryland Gov. Wes Moore said that data center projects must follow his guidelines to receive his support.

The details: In his February State of the State address, Moore said that data center projects seeking his support must hire local workers, engage the community, and cover the cost of their power needs. More recently, he has portrayed Virginia, home to Data Center Alley, as a cautionary tale.

"The way they did it there cannot and will not happen in the state of Maryland," Moore said during an event in August, according to Maryland Matters.

Past views: In 2024, Moore announced that legislation removing regulatory barriers to technology infrastructure was part of his agenda for the legislative session. When he later signed the bill into law, Moore praised what it would mean for the state.

"This bill is going to supercharge the data center industry in Maryland so we can unleash more economic potential and create more good-paying union jobs," Moore said in May 2024.

The explanation: A spokesperson for Moore did not provide a comment to Business Insider.

In August, Texas Gov. Greg Abbott, a Republican, announced an effective pause on data centers seeking to connect to the state's power grid until the Public Utility Commission and Electric Reliability Council of Texas, which operates an independent grid that services the vast majority of the state, conduct a comprehensive audit.

The details: Abbott's order cited the need to ensure ERCOT can keep up with future demand. In a statement explaining the audit, Abbott's office noted that 90% of new power requests are for data centers. Abbott also directed the two entities to gather information about proposed data centers, including their power generation, water consumption, ownership, and the extent to which the projects may need public assistance.

Past views: Abbott previously bragged about his state's ability to attract big projects. In November 2025, he celebrated Google's planned $40 billion investment by saying, "Texas is the epicenter of AI development."

The explanation: Abbott said data center developers had only themselves to blame for the backlash.

"They pop up in places that nobody ever heard of before, until they started the construction," Abbott said on ABC's "This Week" on August 23. "And so they had not been working in collaboration with the state, they'd not been in collaboration with local governments, and so they basically dug their own grave for the problem that's been caused for them, and that's why they got the backlash they deserve."

Florida Republican gubernatorial nominee Byron Donalds' campaign has published an ad saying he would "protect Florida families and communities from data centers."

The details: Donalds, who currently serves in the US House, has introduced legislation that would require data centers to generate their own power and to source their water from outside public systems.

Past views: According to Florida Politics, a digital media site, Donalds previously questioned other candidates who want to pause data center construction.

"There ain't no bans coming," he said.

Donalds' opponent, former Rep. David Jolly, who was previously a Republican and has since switched parties, has pledged to pause hyperscale data center construction for at least one year.

The explanation: A spokesperson for Donalds did not respond to a request for comment from Business Insider.

In May, Utah Gov. Spencer Cox, a Republican, issued an executive order that called for "a higher bar" for data center development.

The details: Cox's order called for state agencies to adopt a framework for considering data centers that focuses on transparency, protecting ratepayers, managing water consumption, and mitigating environmental impacts. Separately, Cox called for reforms to a state agency that pushed what became a controversial data center project.

Past views: Cox was a strong proponent of the Stratos Project, an initially proposed 40,000-acre hyperscale AI data center campus that is backed by "Shark Tank" investor Kevin O'Leary. Cox initially questioned those who criticized the proposal.

"I'm so tired of our country taking years to get stuff done. It's the dumbest thing ever. We think that taking time makes things better or safer, it absolutely does not," Cox said during an April news conference. "You get a chance to give your feedback, and then decisions get made. That's how we have to do stuff in this country and in this state."

The explanation: A spokesperson for Cox did not respond to Business Insider's request for comment. In the wake of the news conference, Cox wrote on X that his statements "did not meet the expectations I have for myself. I seek to do better." He also told reporters that public pressure helped spur his order.

"Public pressure is important, and if I had had any concerns about water and the Great Salt Lake, I would have opposed it from the very beginning," Cox said in June, per local news station KSL. "But the public has brought up some concerns that some of us didn't think about that are important, and that matters."

Sen. Jon Husted of Ohio, a Republican, is sponsoring legislation that would codify elements of President Donald Trump's "Ratepayer Protection Pledge" into law.

The details: In July, Husted introduced legislation requiring states to consider standards for data centers and other large electricity users that consume 100 megawatts or more at a single site or campus. The standards include requiring those customers to cover the cost of grid upgrades needed to serve them.

Past views: As lieutenant governor, Husted celebrated Google's 2024 announcement that it would invest $2.3 billion in the state.

"Data centers are essential to our digital lives and Google's additional multibillion-dollar investment further establishes central Ohio as an important tech hub in America," Husted said in a statement at the time.

The explanation: Sen. Husted's spokesperson said his view had not changed. He sounded a similar note when Spectrum News asked him about his past statements.

"It's not really a shift. I was always trying to hold these companies accountable by making them pay local property taxes… working to make them pay their share of the infrastructure that they're required to… making sure that they hired local labor," he told the news outlet in July. "So this is very consistent for me, holding them accountable."

Ohio Republican gubernatorial nominee Vivek Ramaswamy has promised that if elected, he would pause approval of any new data center project announcements until state lawmakers passed his preferred requirements.

The details: In August, Ramaswamy announced he would issue an executive order to halt "the approval of any new data center project announcements" until his framework was passed into law. His requirements include providing free electricity for homeowners in communities with data centers, requiring data centers to pay full property taxes and then using the revenue to cut Ohio homeowners' property taxes, and requiring the facilities to comply with environmental standards.

"There are hundreds of data centers already across our state, and the pace of construction is accelerating," he said in a statement released by his campaign. "While I had no part in these past projects, I am committed to ensuring our policies catch up to current realities."

Past views: Previously, Ramaswamy said the fast pace of Ohio's data center buildout "was a good thing," provided the grid could keep up.

"We've got AI data centers moving to our state, that's a good thing, that's a good thing, I want the sectors of the future to come here," he said in March 2025. "But that will make a level of demand on our electric grid of a kind that we have not seen in the history of our state."

The explanation: A spokesperson for Ramaswamy did not respond to a request for comment from Business Insider.

text:
As the adoption of electric vehicles (EVs) continues to grow, the disposal of spent EV batteries is emerging as a major social and environmental challenge. Wastewater generated during conventional battery recycling processes can contain high concentrations of heavy metals, posing risks of soil and groundwater contamination.

Cathode materials, which play a key role in determining battery capacity, also contain significant amounts of costly critical metals such as cobalt, whose extraction can cause environmental damage. As a result, direct recycling technologies for spent batteries, which can preserve the existing structure of battery materials while recovering valuable resources, are gaining increasing attention.

Against this backdrop, a research team led by Dr. Jung-Je Woo of the Gwangju Clean Energy Research Center at the Korea Institute of Energy Research (KIER) has developed a technology that completely separates current collectors, one of the major technical challenges in the direct recycling of spent batteries. The team also succeeded in simultaneously regenerating spent cathode materials to a performance level comparable to that of pristine materials.

The key to the newly developed technology lies in the complete separation of the current collector from the cathode material. Current collectors facilitate the flow of electricity within batteries and are strongly bonded to cathode materials so that they remain firmly attached during repeated charging and discharging. During battery recycling, however, this strong adhesion has traditionally required the use of specialized solutions containing hazardous chemicals to dissolve the bonding components. In addition, residual substances generated during this process can remain on the cathode material, potentially degrading the performance of the regenerated electrodes. As a result, current collector separation has remained a major challenge in direct battery recycling.

To overcome this limitation, the research team developed a solution-based recycling process. When spent cathode materials are immersed in a diethylene glycol solution and heated to 130 °C, the diethylene glycol undergoes oxidation to form glycolaldehyde. Because glycolaldehyde readily interacts with other molecules, it weakens the adhesion between the cathode material and the current collector, enabling complete separation of the current collector. At the same time, electrons generated during the oxidation of diethylene glycol facilitate the replenishment of lithium ions in the cathode material, enabling delamination and regeneration occur simultaneously in a single step.

Using the developed process, the researchers regenerated NCM and LFP cathode materials, both widely used in electric vehicles. The regenerated NCM cathode recovered 99.1% of the capacity of pristine material, while the regenerated LFP cathode recovered 99.7%, demonstrating performance nearly equivalent to that of pristine cathode materials.

The researchers also applied the technology to degraded cathode material from a 50-ampere-hour (Ah) EV battery and fabricated it to a small pouch cell using the regenerated material. The discharge capacity increased from 30.6 milliampere-hours (mAh) to 34.6 mAh, demonstrating the potential of the technology for regenerating cathode materials recovered from actual EV batteries.

Dr. Jinju Song of KIER, who led the study, said, "This technology enables spent battery cathode materials to be recycled without dissolving the active material, making it an environmentally friendly approach that can reduce both wastewater-related pollution and energy consumption." She added, "The process is simple and does not require specialized sealed processing environments, giving it strong potential for industrial application."

This research was supported by the Ministry of Trade, Industry and Resources (MOTIR) and the Ministry of Science and ICT (MSIT) of the Republic of Korea. The findings were published in the September 2026 issue of Advanced Science (IF 14.1), a leading international scientific journal.

title: Diablo on Hold | Sierra Club
description:
The legislature nullified legislative approval of the agreement signed six years previously to shut down the Diablo Canyon Nuclear Power Plant by 2025, instead extending its life to 2030.
On July 30, a Diablo 2045 “information panel” at the SLO County Government center featured a dais stacked with nuclear advocates.
As Supervisor Gibson accurately observed when the event was announced, it was “outlined to deliver two purely supportive studies of the economic benefits of continued Diablo Canyon Power Plant operation.
Instead, they’ve repeatedly discouraged and failed to perform such an ongoing evaluation of Diablo Canyon and the alternatives.
Will Diablo Canyon still be needed for energy reliability beyond 2030?
text:
In 2022, Governor Newsom and the California legislature pulled a 180-degree turn in state policy. The legislature nullified legislative approval of the agreement signed six years previously to shut down the Diablo Canyon Nuclear Power Plant by 2025, instead extending its life to 2030.

The relicensing of the plant, previously abandoned, was resurrected in a dash through a truncated version of the normal process for the licensing of a nuclear power plant. Conditions built into the 2030 extension bill – including a full accounting of costs, proof of necessity, assurance of repayment of a large state loan, and an apples-to-apples comparison of the cost of operating Diablo vs. energy from renewable sources, energy efficiency and conservation – have languished. Instead, PG&E, nuclear advocates, and state resource agencies have been swirling walnut shells around on a card table and inviting legislators to guess which one the pea is under.

Almost from the moment Governor Newsom did an about-face on the plan to close Diablo Canyon, there has been a growing drumbeat to extend the life of the plant further -- along with its rising costs, devastating impacts on the marine environment, and ever-growing coastal nuclear waste dump -- out to 2045.

On June 16, a majority of the SLO County Board of Supervisors, as dissenting Supervisor Bruce Gibson put it, “enthusiastically and uncritically” endorsed the longer extension, voting 4-1 to join the “Diablo Canyon 2045 Coalition” of local city councils and chambers of commerce.

On July 30, a Diablo 2045 “information panel” at the SLO County Government center featured a dais stacked with nuclear advocates. As Supervisor Gibson accurately observed when the event was announced, it was “outlined to deliver two purely supportive studies of the economic benefits of continued Diablo Canyon Power Plant operation. That is followed by safety reports from PG&E itself regarding findings on seismic hazard and reactor embrittlement (neither yet peer-reviewed). The final panel comprises stakeholders from the labor, economic development and education communities, whose interests align with continued operations.”

The Diablo 2045 folks were counting on a bill making a speed run through the state legislature at the end of August, just before legislators adjourned for the year. They hoped it would be rammed through with the same inadequate analysis and debate that accompanied the Diablo 2030 extension bill that was passed in the dead of night at the end of the 2022 legislative session.

But an analysis of the embrittlement of one of Diablo’s reactor domes is not expected to be completed until October. And recent data has shown that the most hazardous of the earthquake faults surrounding the plant is capable of producing a more powerful earthquake than previously thought. PG&E somehow has never found the time to respond to an independent peer review panel that would like to know why the utility’s most recent seismic safety update did not mention the most recent data and incorporate it into its analysis. The peer-review panel has been asking for that explanation since February.

Now PG&E will have plenty of time. On August 7, Governor Newsom halted the nuclear giddy-up. There will be no last-minute bill flying through the legislature this year, and Diablo’s fate will be up to the governor who replaces him next year.

PG&E and Diablo Canyon’s cheerleaders have shown a marked preference for brief discussions (or no discussions), vague statements, selective omissions, and tightly controlled information.

Why were nuclear advocates hell-bent on a last-minute policy change to extend Diablo’s life to 2030 with minimal review, and then trying to rush through another one to extend it to 2045? As former Nuclear Regulatory Commissioner and energy policy advisor Peter Bradford has observed, California usually makes decisions about energy generation resources “on the basis of full information and equitable allocation of risks and rewards.” But when it comes to those who are pushing for endless extensions of the life of California’s last nuclear plant:

“If they really believed what they tell the legislature and the public about the benefits of Diablo Canyon extension, they would be at the head of the line of those demanding a prudent, transparent and thorough evaluative process. Instead, they’ve repeatedly discouraged and failed to perform such an ongoing evaluation of Diablo Canyon and the alternatives. This silence, even in the face of the legislature’s clear 2022 mandate speaks volumes as to what they expect the outcome to be…. Now’s the time to establish a genuinely prudent process that will spare the legislature and others from having to make hugely consequential decisions on a crisis basis with severely limited information. That’s the path that legislators should insist on.”

That expert testimony and much more was delivered to two dozen staff from the offices of California legislators who attended an August 14 briefing, “Diablo Canyon Through 2045? What California Lawmakers Need to Know About Regulatory Prudence, Cost and Reliability,” moderated by Kim Delfino, President and Founder of Earth Advocacy, and co-hosted by San Luis Obispo Mothers for Peace, Sierra Club California, California Alliance for Community Energy and California Environmental Justice Coalition.

The expert speakers focused on four central questions:

What would continued operation cost California ratepayers and taxpayers?

Will Diablo Canyon still be needed for energy reliability beyond 2030?

How should changes in federal nuclear regulation and safety oversight factor into the state’s decision?

What standard of prudence and accountability should lawmakers require before approving another extension?

John Geesman, an attorney at Dickson Geesman LLP and former California Energy Commission member, California Power Exchange chair and California ISO board member, spoke on cost, ratepayer and regulatory analysis. Geesman focused on the financial implications of continued operation. He said PG&E forecasts a $595 million deficit for 2027, bringing the cumulative shortfall since extended operations began in November 2024 to $1.7 billion.

“Diablo Canyon is what the financial world calls a ‘stranded asset,’ meaning that the plant persistently falls short of covering its costs with the market revenues it receives for producing electricity,” he said. As a result, it’s clear who will be left covering those costs: “PG&E now admits that its grant payments will fall short by at least $659 million, and its CEO says taxpayers should absorb that loss.” he said.

Mark Z. Jacobson, a Stanford professor of civil and environmental engineering, spoke on energy reliability, renewables and storage, examining Diablo Canyon’s role as California expands solar, wind and battery storage. Jacobson presented data showing that the plant’s inflexible generation is contributing to increased curtailment of renewable energy.

“Diablo Canyon is forcing wind and solar off the grid,” Jacobson said, “so you’re just paying for wasted electricity.” He summed up the data this way: “The direction is clear that renewables decrease electricity prices; fossil fuels and nuclear increase prices on grids.”

Edwin Lyman, the Director of Nuclear Power Safety at the Union of Concerned Scientists, spoke on nuclear safety, security and NRC oversight and what changes at the U.S. Nuclear Regulatory Commission (NRC) under Trump could mean for federal oversight of Diablo Canyon. He noted a pattern of reduced inspections, unresolved seismic risks and potential changes to safety and security requirements.

“Every state, California included, that has operating nuclear power plants needs to understand that they can no longer rely on the federal agency, the NRC, to protect public health, safety and the environment,” he said.

Peter Bradford, a former NRC commissioner and former chair of the Maine and New York utility commissions, spoke on prudence, licensing and regulatory accountability. Bradford criticized the California Public Utilities Commission for failing to adequately assess the costs, risks, benefits and alternatives to continued operation for the five-year extended term through 2030 and cautioned that a thorough analysis was essential before considering another extension.

“Prudence has been a crucial customer protection term in utility regulation for the last 100 years,” he said. “The requirement that customers not pay for imprudently incurred costs is the ultimate safeguard against imposition of costs that have not been adequately evaluated or controlled.”

title: EV Tax Credits and Incentives: Complete Guide | Bright Coding
description:
How the federal EV tax credit works in 2026 The federal credit (officially the Clean Vehicle Credit) is the anchor of EV incentives in the US.
Can I use the EV tax credit if I don't owe taxes?
Do I qualify for the EV tax credit if I buy a Tesla?
Can I get both the used and new EV tax credits?
Conclusion EV incentives in 2026 are generous but bureaucratic, and the money goes to buyers who prepare.
text:
A $40,000 EV that costs you $33,500 is a very different purchase from one that costs the sticker price. That's the power of EV tax credits and incentives — and it's also where thousands of buyers quietly lose money every year by missing a deadline, buying a car that doesn't qualify, or skipping a rebate they were owed. This guide walks you through the 2026 rules, step by step.

TL;DR — Key Takeaways

The federal clean vehicle credit can be worth up to $7,500 on new EVs, and up to $4,000 on qualifying used EVs.

You can now transfer the credit to the dealer at the point of sale, so the discount shows up immediately instead of next April.

Eligibility hinges on three things: where the car was made, its MSRP, and your personal income.

State and local incentives stack on top of federal ones — some buyers combine them for $10,000+ total savings.

The single most common mistake is assuming a qualifying vehicle automatically qualifies for you.

How the federal EV tax credit works in 2026

The federal credit (officially the Clean Vehicle Credit) is the anchor of EV incentives in the US. For a new EV, it's worth up to $7,500, split into two $3,750 halves — one for critical battery minerals and one for battery components — both of which must be sourced from approved countries and suppliers.

Think of the credit like a coupon that has to survive two checkpoints. If the car's battery minerals and components both pass, you get the full $7,500. If only one passes, you get $3,750. If neither passes, you get nothing. That's why two EVs at the same price can earn completely different credits.

Which EVs qualify changes constantly as manufacturers shift suppliers. Tesla, GM, Ford, Hyundai, and others have models on the current IRS list, but the list updates throughout the year. Always check the IRS's official qualified vehicle list before you negotiate, not after.

Eligibility: the four rules that decide your credit

Requirement New EV credit Used EV credit Maximum vehicle price (MSRP) $55,000 for cars; $80,000 for trucks/SUVs $25,000 sale price Battery sourcing Must pass mineral + component checkpoints No sourcing requirement Buyer income cap $150,000 single / $300,000 married filing jointly $75,000 single / $150,000 married filing jointly Must buy from A registered dealer, new vehicle A registered dealer, must be 2+ model years old

For the used EV credit, the cap is 30% of the sale price or $4,000, whichever is lower. A $13,000 used Leaf nets you $3,900. A $24,000 used car nets you the full $4,000. The car must be at least two model years old, it must have a clean title, and you must not be claimed as a dependent on someone else's taxes.

Point-of-sale transfer: get the discount now

The rule that changed everything: since 2024, you can transfer your federal credit to the dealership, and the dealer applies it directly to your purchase price. No waiting for tax season, no worrying whether you have enough tax liability to absorb a non-refundable credit.

Here's how it plays out: a teacher in Ohio found a qualifying 2026 EV at $46,000. She transferred the full $7,500 credit to the dealer, financed $38,500, and walked out the same day — the discount was already baked into her loan. The dealer then claims the credit on their own return after filing the required paperwork with the IRS.

The caveat: the credit is still subject to your income limits, and if the IRS later determines you were ineligible, you may owe the credit back. Know your income bracket before you claim it, even with the point-of-sale transfer.

State and local incentives stack on top

The federal credit is only the first layer. States add their own rebates, and they vary wildly. California offers a Clean Vehicle Rebate with income-based tiers; Colorado's EV credit combined with federal incentives has pushed the effective price of some EVs below $25,000. Other states, including many without their own rebates, still offer perks like HOV lane access, free parking, and reduced registration fees.

Electric utility companies are the quiet third layer. Many utilities offer $500–$2,000 rebates on home charger installation or discounted overnight charging rates. A Portland couple combined a federal credit, an Oregon rebate, and a utility charger rebate to cut the total cost of their new EV by more than $10,000 — that's the "stacking" strategy in action.

Before you buy, check three sources: your state's energy or motor-vehicle agency website, your local utility's rebate page, and the federal Department of Energy's incentive database. These programs have limited funds and expire — usually on a first-come, first-served basis.

The 5-year cost math nobody does

Incentives matter most when you run the full ownership numbers. Consider two realistic scenarios:

Qualifying new EV Non-qualifying new EV Sticker price $45,000 $45,000 Federal credit (transferred) –$7,500 $0 State rebate (varies) –$2,000 (typical) $0 Home charger rebate –$750 (typical) $0 Effective purchase price $34,750 $45,000

Same car, different VIN, different battery supplier — a $10,000 gap. That's why the smartest EV shoppers make the incentives list the first filter, not the last.

Mistakes that cost buyers thousands

Assuming the car qualifies before checking the IRS list. Battery sourcing rules change mid-year. Confirm on the official list on the day you buy.

Missing the income cap. The credit is a one-time benefit per vehicle and per buyer, and the used-EV credit can only be claimed once every three years.

Buying from a private seller and losing the credit. Used-EV incentives generally require a licensed dealer. That amazing Craigslist deal forfeits the $4,000.

Leasing the wrong way. On a lease, the manufacturer (not you) owns the car and usually claims the commercial credit — negotiate a lower lease payment to capture that value instead of assuming you'll get anything.

Ignoring the transfer paperwork. The dealer must report the sale to the IRS; if they skip it, your point-of-sale discount can be clawed back. Confirm the paperwork is filed before you sign.

Can I use the EV tax credit if I don't owe taxes? The new EV credit is non-refundable but transferable to the dealer, so even buyers with no tax liability can benefit by taking the point-of-sale discount — the dealer absorbs the credit. How much is the EV tax credit for a used car in 2026? Up to $4,000 or 30% of the sale price, whichever is lower, provided the car is under $25,000, is two or more model years old, and you meet the income limits.

Who Is This For / Not For

Who this is for: Anyone buying or leasing a new or used EV in the US who wants to legally minimize the real purchase price, and buyers deciding between multiple EVs where incentives tip the scale.

Who this is not for: Drivers in countries without equivalent incentives (rules here are US-specific), buyers of vehicles over the price caps, and high-income earners above the credit thresholds — for you, negotiate the price instead of chasing a credit you can't use.

FAQ

Do EV tax credits apply to leases? Usually not directly to you — the manufacturer owns the leased vehicle and can claim the commercial credit, so the discount should appear in your monthly payment. Ask the dealer to show you the credit in the lease terms.

What happens if the EV tax credit runs out? Some state rebates do run out of funds mid-year. The federal credit is tied to vehicle qualification, not a set pot, so it continues as long as qualifying vehicles and buyers exist.

Do I qualify for the EV tax credit if I buy a Tesla? Possibly — several Tesla models are on the qualified list, but trim level and MSRP must stay under the caps, and your income must be within the limits.

Can I get both the used and new EV tax credits? No, and the used credit can only be claimed once every three years. Each credit also requires the vehicle's first use to be in the US.

Conclusion

EV incentives in 2026 are generous but bureaucratic, and the money goes to buyers who prepare. Start with the IRS qualified-vehicle list, confirm your income bracket, check your state and utility rebates, and use the point-of-sale transfer so the federal credit hits your price the day you buy. Five minutes of checking can put $10,000 back in your pocket — which is exactly what the programs were designed to reward.

text:
Data released by the Federation of Automobile Dealers Associations (FADA), the apex automobile dealers' governing body in India, has revealed that total vehicle retail registrations in August 2026 reached 24,23,201 units, marking a 17.51% year-on-year (YoY) growth over the corresponding period last year. However, the month-on-month (MoM) retail sales slipped 6.48% in August 2026 owing to seasonal monsoon patterns and calendar shifts that moved festival buying into September this year.

Total passenger vehicle retail reached 402,398 units last month, registering a 16.14% YoY growth. This propelled the industry to clock the four lakh milestone in August for the first time. In this record retail sales performance, CNG cars contributed a 25.28% share, while hybrids secured 9.04%. On the other hand, electric vehicles accounted for 7.63% of the total passenger vehicle retail sales last month. This shift towards alternative fuel comes at a time when, across the broader market, total electric vehicle sales reached 298,448 units, taking overall EV penetration to 12.3%.

Dealers noted that running costs and buyer hesitation regarding the E20 petrol transition directed demand toward alternative fuel options, even as petrol remained the largest standalone fuel category. FADA also revealed that rural passenger vehicle sales in August expanded 24.99% compared to 10.93% in urban regions.

Meanwhile, inventory levels in passenger vehicles expanded by five days over July to reach 38 to 40 days, well above the recommended 21-day mark. FADA cautioned that showroom conversion during the September-to-November festive window will determine seasonal stability as dealerships navigate elevated stock levels and scheduled vehicle price revisions.

Speaking on the August retail performance, FADA President Sai Giridhar identified the historic shift in passenger vehicle powertrains as the defining element of the performance. "The defining development of the month, however, was a structural one: for the first time in India’s history, alternative fuels — CNG, hybrid and electric combined — overtook petrol in the Passenger Vehicle market, at 41.95% against petrol’s 40.85%," he said, while adding that a little over a year ago petrol led this contest by nearly 11% points but that lead has now been erased.

Tractors remained flat, with 0.84% growth to 87,977 units, declining 25.03% MoM amid a 13% monsoon deficit across 14 states, ANI reported.

Sanders Wants Superintelligence Banned

The legislation would permanently prohibit the development and deployment of superintelligent AI while temporarily pausing advanced AI development until a federal regulator establishes safety standards.

It would also call for international agreements to prevent superintelligence from being developed globally. The proposal has already drawn criticism from investors and technology policy advocates.

Pershing Square founder Bill Ackman argued that halting U.S. development could allow geopolitical rivals to reach superintelligence first.

Sanders’ AI Push Expands to Data Centers, Public Ownership

Sanders has also pushed for a national data-center moratorium, later working with Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-N.Y.) to put the idea into legislation. While initially facing resistance from Democrats, similar calls have since gained bipartisan support.

Texas Gov. Greg Abbott (R) has halted new data-center approvals pending reviews of their water and power needs, while Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro (D) now requires local approval for new projects.

In June, Sanders proposed giving the public ownership stakes in major AI labs, with the government having a say in deployment decisions. The idea echoes proposals from Anthropic and OpenAI.

Last week, Nvidia Corp (NASDAQ:NVDA) CEO Jensen Huang urged regulators to focus on real-world risks, saying, "Don’t regulate hypothetical theoretical harm, regulate actual and pragmatic harm."

text:
As electric vehicle (EV) sales in China and North America continue to decline, global automakers are reshaping their market focus toward Europe and Asia. Chinese automakers such as BYD and Geely are maintaining their sales dominance.

According to SNE Research, the global EV delivery volume reached a total of 11.8 million units from January to July 2026, reflecting a 6.3% increase compared to the same period last year.

BYD sold 1.81 million units, down 17.9% from the same period last year, but managed to retain its position as the number one seller. Despite sluggish domestic demand in China, it is believed that overseas expansion—focused on Europe, Southeast Asia, and Central and South America—helped limit the extent of the overall decline.

Geely rose to second place with 1.17 million units, an increase of 1.6%. Tesla followed with 940,000 units, up 12.8%, and Volkswagen ranked next with 780,000 units, an increase of 2.8%.

China's SAIC sold 720,000 units, Changan sold 500,000 units, while Chery continued its export growth with 460,000 units.

Hyundai Motor Group recorded 440,000 units, marking a significant year-on-year growth of 24.2% among the top players. Recovery in European sales and growing demand in Asia contributed to the improved performance.

By region, China retained its position as the world's largest EV market with 6.36 million units, but this represented an 8.2% drop compared to the same period last year.

Europe saw its EV sales grow by 29.2% to 2.96 million units, increasing its market share from 20.7% to 25.1%. Stricter emission regulations, the introduction of affordable new models, and government incentives in various countries fueled demand.

North America performed the weakest among major regions, with sales plunging 22.7% to 790,000 units. The end of tax credits as of the end of September 2025 increased the purchasing burden, and a combination of high vehicle prices due to tariffs further delayed demand recovery.

Asia (excluding China) became the fastest growing market, surging 77.0% to 1.11 million units. Policy support, the launch of new models, and local production in countries such as South Korea, India, and nations in Southeast Asia all contributed to this rapid growth. Other regions—including Central and South America and the Middle East—also achieved robust growth, with sales reaching 560,000 units, up 158.1%.

SNE Research stated, "In the second half of the year, the scope of demand adjustment in China, whether the tax credit gap in the U.S. will persist, and the sustainability of Europe’s growth will determine the market direction. The pace of localization and the ability to supply affordable models will be key variables in market share changes for the remainder of the year."

text:
On-site meeting at the Louisiana steel plant

Amid the global manufacturing drive for “carbon neutrality”

World’s first to cut carbon emissions by 70%

Outlook for recovering previously shrunken sales volumes to the U.S.

A bird’s-eye view of the Hyundai Steel–POSCO Louisiana (HPLS) electric arc furnace steel mill located on the Mississippi River in Donaldsonville, Louisiana, USA. Provided by Hyundai Steel

“When our steel mill begins producing steel sheets in the first quarter of 2029 (January to March), it will become the world’s first steel mill to reduce carbon emissions by 70% compared with blast furnace operations.”

Hyunghin Kim, CEO of the Hyundai Steel–POSCO Louisiana (HPLS) joint venture, stressed this point on 3 September (local time) at a press briefing held at the HPLS electric arc furnace steel mill site in Donaldsonville, Louisiana, USA. The mill is the Korean steel industry’s first steel plant in the United States, being built by Hyundai Steel and other Hyundai Motor Group affiliates together with POSCO Group at a cost of USD 5.8 billion (approximately KRW 7.8 trillion). It is also the first integrated electric arc furnace steel mill in the United States.

After operations begin, the plant is projected to generate annual sales of USD 4.0 billion (approximately KRW 5.4 trillion). This is because it will produce high value-added low-carbon steel and will have a large-scale annual production capacity of 2.7 million tons. In particular, the flagship product—automotive steel sheets, which will account for two-thirds of total output—is expected to sell smoothly as global automakers seek to procure such materials to implement carbon neutrality policies.

● “Will become a game changer for low-carbon steel sheets”

Hyundai Steel’s decision to disclose projected sales even before construction starts reflects its strong confidence in the products to be manufactured. As countries worldwide work to reduce carbon emissions, the global automotive industry is seeking a breakthrough in body steel sheets for carbon reduction, recognizing that a shift to electric vehicles alone is insufficient. Taeckjun Kim, head of Hyundai Steel’s North America Steel Business Strategy Office (Managing Director), who also attended the event, expressed confidence, saying, “HPLS will become a ‘game changer’ in the field of low-carbon steel sheets.”

The HPLS electric arc furnace steel mill is also significant in terms of technology. It marks the debut on the global stage of the Korean steel industry’s “green steel” technologies. This is the first time a domestic steelmaker will produce steel using a “double eco-friendly” process that combines natural gas-based direct reduced iron (DRI) with electric arc furnaces. High-purity iron in the form of DRI is produced not by melting iron ore, but by blowing natural gas at high temperature to selectively remove only the oxygen. The resulting DRI is then charged into an electric arc furnace together with steel scrap and reborn as high-quality molten steel.

Regarding the timing of a future transition to a “zero carbon emission” DRI process using hydrogen instead of natural gas, Managing Director Kim said, “The timing of hydrogen use is still under review, as we must assess its economic feasibility.”

● Will US sales recover after tariff-driven contraction?

Once this steel mill is built, exports to the United States, which had contracted due to the 50% tariff imposed on Korean steel, are expected to naturally recover. Last year, Korea’s steel exports to the US were 2.54 million tons, down 8% from 2.76 million tons the previous year, indicating a continuing decline. CEO Kim explained, “Because of the impact of tariffs, the volume previously exported from Korean plants to the US has significantly decreased,” adding, “With the construction of this steel mill, steel sales are expected to exceed the amount lost to export declines.”

Some outlets for HPLS production have already been secured. For automotive steel sheets, supply volumes to Hyundai Motor and Kia’s US plants (800,000 tons) have been finalized, and POSCO has agreed to sell 600,000 tons to its existing US customers. José Muñoz, President and Global COO of Hyundai Motor Company, told reporters at the HPLS groundbreaking ceremony on 4 September, “We are in discussions with some local automakers.” CEO Kim said, “As sustainability has become a core agenda item not only for automakers but for the global manufacturing industry as a whole, carbon reduction will be a major competitive edge in securing customers.”

text:
The federal government has quietly shelved a 2023 promise to implement national packaging standards aimed at curbing plastic waste, citing concern for increasing cost of living pressures.

In an email to stakeholders, the Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water last week said the mandatory standards would not go ahead in this term of government.

Instead, it will work with the states and territories on "opportunities to improve" packaging standards.

"The Minister is looking at the pursuit of reforms in a way that balances environmental outcomes with the broader needs of the economy, with the Government looking closely at its policies to ensure it does not exacerbate cost of living pressures," the email said.

"The Minister has communicated that a new Commonwealth scheme for packaging will not be introduced in this term of government and is now focused on working with state and territory governments on opportunities to improve Australia's packaging regulations and policies in the nearer term."

Federal Environment Minister Murray Watt told the ABC in a statement that the Albanese government remains committed to "delivering stronger environmental outcomes".

"Our immediate focus is to work with state and territory governments to reduce waste by harmonising packaging and recycling policy in Australia," he said.

State and territory environment ministers struck a deal in June 2023 with then federal environment minister, Tanya Plibersek, to implement packaging standards, including minimum targets for recycled products in packaging and limiting the use of harmful chemicals in food wrappers.

A press release issued at the time said it was "clear that voluntary targets and design guidelines aren't working".

The minimum standards for the Commonwealth packaging scheme had not been finalised prior to the plan being scrapped.

But national targets set in 2018 included having an average of 50 per cent of recycled content in packaging.

Only 28 per cent of rigid plastics and 9 per cent of soft plastics were reused, recycled or reclaimed in the most recent Australian Packaging Consumption and Recovery data, from 2023-24.

Recycling industry 'devastated' by broken promise

Many in the recycling and sustainability industries say they were blindsided by the decision, which followed years of consultations and sustained pressure by the states and territories.

Managing director of sustainability and waste management consulting firm MRA Consulting, Mike Ritchie, said the national standards had been agreed to multiple times by different levels of governments.

"[We've] gone down different paths of intergovernmental agreements and looking at how to do it," he said.

Mr Ritchie said failing to have national standards could mean different packaging and labelling rules in all eight states and territories.

CEO of the Australian Council of Recycling, Suzanne Toumbourou, said a lack of certainty around packaging reforms left Australian manufacturers at risk of closure.

"Australian plastic recycling facilities are operating at around half their available capacity on average," Ms Toumbourou said.

"Without those obligations, Australian recyclers are left competing on a vastly uneven playing field with cheap imported plastic."

Last week one of Australia's biggest recycling businesses, Recycling Plastics Australia, went into voluntary administration, leaving around 60 jobs up in the air.

The company received $20 million in federal funding in 2024 to accelerate the recycling of soft plastics, under the Recycling Modernisation Fund.

"Without packaging reform, we will continue throwing away plastic packaging while importing more of it, even as the domestic recycling capacity Australia has worked so hard to build begins to shrink," Ms Toumbourou said.

Independent MP Kate Chaney said the government's decision to walk away from the proposed reform was "deeply disappointing".

"Industry wants certainty, communities want the pollution to stop, and both point to the same reform. This is a rare moment of alignment, and the government is letting it pass."

Fellow independent MP Sophie Scamps said the federal government has "broken another promise" by backing down on the proposed reforms.

"The government's decision is nonsensical. With both industry and environmental groups on board this would have been an easy win.

"Instead they're jumping at shadows," Dr Scamps said.

Cost of living argument questioned

Mr Ritchie said the federal government has not conducted a regulatory impact statement on a proposed Commonwealth packaging scheme.

A regulatory impact statement looks at the economic, social and environmental costs of proposed government regulation.

"[The government] can make no prognostications, no arguments, no pros and cons of packaging reform without having done it," he said.

Mr Ritchie said modelling he had done with the Australian Packaging Covenant Organisation found mandatory recycling standards would cost around 0.3 cents per packaging item.

Minister Watt's office did not respond to questions from the ABC about what economic modelling the government had undertaken to determine cost of living pressures would increase under a mandatory packaging scheme.

Greens spokesperson for waste and the circular economy, Steph Hodgins-May, said any costs associated with the scheme may be offset by the environmental benefits.

"We're also hearing that there would be significant cost savings to be made through council rates because there would significantly less waste to be collected," Senator Hodgins-May said.

Independent MP Kate Chaney said kerbside collection and council clean-ups cost ratepayers between $70 and $95 a year.

"The government points to cost of living, but the numbers don't support that," Ms Chaney said.

Senator Hodgins-May said the government has failed to provide evidence that cost is a barrier to implementing mandatory standards.

"Until they do, we think that there is no excuse to continue letting these corporations pollute and plunder and making that responsibility fall onto consumers."

Senator Hodgins-May pointed to public support to act on plastics pollution.

Polling from the Australian Marine Conservation Society released in June this year found that nine in ten people surveyed want stronger action to curb single-use plastics, and more than six in ten (63 per cent) want mandatory packaging laws to replace voluntary targets.

"It's one of the many areas where the public are demanding action and they are scratching their heads saying, why isn't the government acting?" she said.

Senator Hodgins-May said the Greens will be campaigning alongside conservation and sustainability groups to get the government to reverse its decision.

"We're at a time now, I think, where all of the ducks are lined up. We've even got industry and the Food and Grocery Council and the like lining up with everyday people saying, now's the time to act."

“The current situation reinforces the importance of building resilience into automotive supply chains that continue to rely on complex global sourcing strategies,” said Daniel Harrison, senior automotive analyst at Ultima Media. “Today, supply chain strategy is increasingly focused on resilience, visibility, and flexibility and these are increasingly becoming fundamental design principles in modern automotive logistics networks.”

But this renewed focus on resilience is not the only way in which the market is changing. The future of automotive logistics in North America will be shaped partly by regulatory decisions made in the next few years. Tariffs and trade uncertainty continue to be a significant hurdle, catalysing the acceleration of regionalisation and localisation strategies throughout the continent. After the US declined to renew the US-Mexico-Canada Agreement (USMCA) on July 1 this year, the three nations will now have annual reviews of the agreement, generating further uncertainty and requiring supply chains to be flexible and agile as tensions grow in North America.

Environmental factors should not be ignored either, with the US Environmental Protection Agency's (EPA) Phase 3 greenhouse gas standards taking effect from 2027. Regulations such as this and California's Advanced Clean Fleets requirements are expected to increasing pressure on fleet operators to invest in transitioning to low- and zero-emission commercial vehicles.

This has been evident in recent M&A activity, including Proficient Auto Logistics’ $130 million acquisition of Hansen & Adkins in the vehicle logistics space and Union Pacific's proposed $85 billion acquisition of Norfolk Southern to create America’s first transcontinental railroad.

And as Harrison identified in the report, labour shortages remain a significant challenge for the North American automotive logistics sector. He noted that persistent shortages of qualifies commercial drivers are continuing to constrain transport capacity and are placing additional upward pressure on wages. The industry has addressed this challenge head-on through investment in a wide range of recruitment initiatives but the issue remains, further compounded by growing demand for technological specialists as the journey towards digitalisation accelerates.

Likewise, the shift towards electrification requires not just EV specialists but also the right infrastructure to enable EV adoption, transport of EVs and widespread use of electric trucks.
