text:
Nairobi, 07 September 2026 – Every US$1 invested in tackling climate change and air pollution together can generate around US$15 in economic benefits, according to a report published today by the UN Environment Programme (UNEP) and the Climate and Clean Air Coalition (CCAC). This is higher than tackling climate and clean air separately, and it includes both market and non-market economic gains.

Released on the International Day of Clean Air for blue skies, Hidden assets: The economic and health case for climate and clean air action is the first comprehensive global economic assessment of integrated climate and clean-air action.

“For too long, we have treated climate action as a cost to be managed and air pollution as the unfortunate outcome of development. This report shows the opposite: clean air is a key driver of development, health, food and energy security, and climate stability – an asset we must invest in,” said Inger Andersen, Executive Director of UNEP. “Proven solutions already exist. What we lack is the decisive leadership from governments, financial institutions, and businesses to deliver them with the speed and coordination this crisis demands.”

The economic value of action

The annual economic benefits of implementing 25 measures that this report identified would be equivalent to:

2.8 per cent of global GDP in 2035

4.5 per cent of global GDP in 2050

11.4 per cent of global GDP in 2100

In comparison, 2.18 per cent of global GDP was spent on explicit fossil fuel subsidies in 2022 and 9.3 per cent of global GDP was spent on healthcare in 2023.

Every year of delayed action would forgo more than US$1.5 trillion annually - 0.5 per cent of GDP - in combined market and non-market benefits.

Even excluding non-market welfare benefits, the measures return around US$4 for every US$1 invested.

“A benefit-cost ratio of 15 to 1 would attract capital instantly in almost any other sector. The only reason it hasn’t on integrated climate and clean air action yet is that the returns are split across health systems, productivity and avoided climate damage rather than landing on a single balance sheet. Every year of delay costs the world more than USD1.5 trillion in benefits we will not get back. Finance ministries and investors who keep climate and air quality in separate budget lines are leaving trillions on the table,” said Elliott Harris, independent, co-chair of the Assessment.

The human cost of air pollution

The US$15 return includes measurable market benefits – such as lower healthcare expenditure, greater labour productivity, and avoided physical damage – and the monetary value of fewer premature deaths and healthier lives.

In 2025, exposure to human-caused outdoor air pollution (PM2.5 and ozone) was linked to an estimated 6.4 million premature deaths worldwide. Household air pollution was linked to a further 2 million premature deaths, including around 300,000 children.

Unlike previous assessments, the report factors in the economic effects of air pollution-related illness, including pressure on health services, losses to productivity and well-being. In 2025, outdoor air pollution contributed to 5.5 million new cases of childhood asthma, 2 million new cases of dementia and millions of cases of heart attack, pulmonary disease, diabetes, stroke and lung cancer.

A package of 25 proven measures

The package of measures examined in the report spans six sectors - energy and fossil fuel systems, industry, transport, agriculture and food systems, residential cooking and heating, and waste management – and combines both long-term decarbonisation measures and measures that target super pollutants such as methane, black carbon, and hydrofluorocarbons (HFCs).

Measures include renewable power and energy efficiency, increasing clean cooking and heating solutions, tighter vehicle emission and efficiency standards, inspection and maintenance, electric vehicles and low-sulfur shipping fuels, recovery of associated gas to end routine venting and flaring and reduce oil and gas leaks, livestock and manure management, more efficient fertilizer use, improved rice cultivation and alternatives to crop residue burning, better solid waste and wastewater management, and phasing down HFCs.

By 2050, full implementation of the 25 measures could cumulatively prevent 144 million air pollution related premature deaths, including 96 million from ambient air pollution alone, and hundreds of millions of cases of chronic disease.

Many deliver domestic health and economic benefits within a single term of government.

Air quality and climate gains

Compared with the report’s baseline scenario, immediate implementation of the measures would halve global carbon dioxide emissions by 2050, reduce methane emissions by 60 per cent and cut major air pollutants – including black carbon, sulphur dioxide, and nitrogen oxides — by around 70 per cent.

The measures would avoid approximately 0.34°C of global warming by 2050 and 1.4°C by 2100. Because land temperature rises faster than the global average, avoided warming in most regions would be greater, reaching an estimated 1.5–2°C by 2100. By the end of the century, carbon dioxide emissions under the scenario would be net negative, while major air pollutants would fall by up to 85 per cent.

“This report provides the most rigorous evidence yet that treating climate change and air pollution as separate problems causes us to underestimate the benefits of tackling either. When we modelled them together, the returns were larger than each could show alone, because the same sources, sectors and policies so often drive both,” said Simon Dietz, Co-Chair of the Assessment and Professor of Environmental Policy, London School of Economics.

The economic value of cleaner air materializes quickly enough to outweigh the implementation cost within a decade and continues to make up almost half of the total economic benefits in 2100, as detailed in the report.

Closing the implementation gap

Institutional barriers – including fragmented decision-making, limited enforcement capacity, and weak government coordination – are the most significant of the implementation barriers identified.

Cumulatively, these barriers risk delaying full implementation by almost eight years globally. Addressing them including through fiscal policy incentives and regulation that enable private sector to roll out technologies that are both profitable and reduce emissions, could accelerate deployment and unlock up to US$10 trillion in additional health benefits by 2040.

This report calls for integrated climate, air-quality, health and economic planning, stronger institutions and enforcement, and better alignment of public and private finance

NOTES TO EDITORS

About the United Nations Environment Programme (UNEP)

The UN Environment Programme is the leading global voice on the environment. It provides leadership and encourages partnership in caring for the environment by inspiring, informing, and enabling nations and peoples to improve their quality of life without compromising that of future generations.

About the Climate and Clean Air Coalition (CCAC)

The Climate and Clean Air Coalition (CCAC) is a voluntary partnership of governments, intergovernmental organizations, businesses, scientific institutions and civil society organizations committed to improving air quality and protecting the climate through actions to reduce short-lived climate pollutants. Its global network includes hundreds of state and non-state partners, and hundreds of local actors carrying out activities across economic sectors. CCAC is also the Secretariat to the Global Methane Pledge. The CCAC Secretariat and Trust Fund are hosted by UNEP.

What The EPA EIS Review Proposal Changed EPA EIS Review Timelines And Page Limits EPA’s June 2026 proposal sought to cap final environmental impact statements at 150 pages, or 300 pages for actions of extraordinary complexity.
The EPA EIS Review proposal uses past timing and length data to support that shift.
The July 1, 2026, EPA proposal on minor New Source Review permits sits beside this debate.
What EPA EIS Review Means For Oversight The practical test for EPA EIS Review is whether speed and transparency can move together.
The June 2026 proposal gives EPA clearer deadlines, shorter document targets, revised definitions and a narrower approach to effects analysis.
text:
The EPA EIS Review changes proposed on June 24, 2026, marked a formal attempt by the Environmental Protection Agency to shorten environmental documentation, set clearer review limits and revise how the agency comments on major federal actions. The proposal was not described in the research record as a final rule as of September 7, 2026, so its practical effect remains partly unresolved. EPA said the package would streamline National Environmental Policy Act procedures, including page limits and a two-year maximum review period for environmental impact statements in most cases, according to the agency’s June 24 proposal.

The stated aim is faster decision-making. The oversight question is whether shorter documents and tighter schedules produce clearer records, or whether they reduce the space available for public scrutiny, environmental justice concerns and interagency disagreement. The available documents support both the administrative direction and the source of concern: EPA proposed defined limits, while also modifying comment procedures and public participation timing.

What The EPA EIS Review Proposal Changed

EPA EIS Review Timelines And Page Limits

EPA’s June 2026 proposal sought to cap final environmental impact statements at 150 pages, or 300 pages for actions of extraordinary complexity. The proposal also sought to enforce a maximum two-year period for completing an EIS. Those limits are tied to the agency’s view that long documents and open-ended schedules can slow permitting and dilute the usefulness of environmental analysis.

The EPA EIS Review proposal uses past timing and length data to support that shift. The research record cites Council on Environmental Quality analysis showing that final EISs from 2019 through 2024 averaged 2.8 years from Notice of Intent to final EIS, while the 2024 average was 2.2 years. It also cites CEQ figures showing that draft and final EISs from 2013 through 2018 averaged 575 pages and 661 pages, respectively. Those figures help explain why EPA framed page and time limits as central to the reform package.

Narrower Effects Analysis

The proposal also clarified that NEPA analysis should focus on the proposed action and reasonably foreseeable environmental effects. It would move away from analysis of speculative or weakly connected indirect effects. That may make documents easier to read and defend administratively, but it also raises a policy question: how agencies will decide when an effect is too remote to analyze.

That boundary matters for climate policy and environmental justice. Large infrastructure decisions can involve emissions, local air quality, water effects, land disturbance and cumulative community burdens. The research record does not establish how EPA will apply the revised standard in specific projects. Until applied in actual reviews, the difference between a clearer scope and a narrower record remains uncertain.

Transparency And Public Participation

Public Comment Flexibility

Draft regulatory amendments published in Federal Register Vol. 91, No. 121 on June 25, 2026, proposed changes to EPA’s NEPA procedures, including definitions such as “applicant,” “connected action” and “environmental document.” The notice also described changes affecting affected-environment analysis, degree-of-effects review, supplemental review triggers and public comment processes, as shown in the Federal Register proposal.

One notable change would allow EPA to publish and seek comment on draft environmental assessments, findings of no significant impact or environmental impact statements when EPA determines that doing so would assist NEPA and other statutory responsibilities. That differs from stricter timing requirements in existing procedures. The agency’s position is that flexibility can reduce unnecessary process. The transparency risk is that discretionary public comment can make participation less predictable for communities that rely on fixed notice periods.

Categorical Exclusions And Review Triggers

The proposed revisions also address categorical exclusions, often called CATEX. The research notes describe changes to how extraordinary circumstances apply, how documentation is handled and how EPA may add, amend or remove exclusions. These provisions matter because categorical exclusions can allow actions to move forward without a full environmental assessment or EIS when significant impacts are not expected.

The proposal is framed as streamlining, but it does not remove the need to consider extraordinary circumstances when impacts may be significant. That distinction is central. A faster exclusion process can reduce paperwork for low-impact actions, while a poorly applied exclusion can reduce public visibility into actions that may affect health, water, habitat or local emissions. The final legal and policy effect depends on the exact final text and agency application.

Oversight Under Clean Air Act Section 309

Comment Letters Under The New Memo

On June 24, 2026, EPA also released an implementation memorandum on comment letters under Clean Air Act Section 309 and NEPA Section 102(2)(C). The research record states that the memo directs comment letters to be clear, timely, confined to EPA’s statutory authority and actionable. It also states that EPA updated its Section 309 review resources on the same date, including reviewer roles and responsibilities, superseding earlier July 2025 guidance.

That matters because Section 309 gives EPA a review function for major federal actions with environmental impacts. A shorter, more focused letter can be easier for a lead agency to address. It can also make EPA’s objections or recommendations more visible to the public. EarthTimes has separately tracked related changes in EPA EIS review updates under the Clean Air Act, where the same tension appears: speed can aid accountability if it produces specific comments, but can weaken oversight if concerns are screened out too early.

For readers who follow policy analysis across connected platforms, Peiknet is a resourceful site belonging to the same broader network.

Policy Stakes For Climate And Justice

Efficiency Versus Record Quality

The climate policy stakes are not limited to document length. EIS documents often form the administrative record for decisions involving energy, transportation, land use, industrial facilities and federal approvals. A record that is shorter but clearer may help agencies and the public identify the main environmental tradeoffs. A record that is shorter because issues were excluded may leave affected communities with fewer tools to understand the decision.

The justice implications are similar. Communities facing pollution burdens often use NEPA comment periods to raise local knowledge about health, traffic, water, cultural resources and emergency response capacity. The research record confirms proposed flexibility in public comment procedures, but it does not confirm how EPA will implement that flexibility project by project. That distinction should be kept clear: the rulemaking proposal is documented; its community-level effects are not yet established.

The July 1, 2026, EPA proposal on minor New Source Review permits sits beside this debate. The research notes state that EPA proposed eliminating minimum federal public participation requirements for minor pollution sources, leaving more discretion to state and local agencies over comment timing and duration. Although that action is separate from the EIS proposal, it points to a broader permitting direction: more discretion for agencies and potentially less uniformity for public notice.

What EPA EIS Review Means For Oversight

The practical test for EPA EIS Review is whether speed and transparency can move together. The June 2026 proposal gives EPA clearer deadlines, shorter document targets, revised definitions and a narrower approach to effects analysis. It also changes how public comment opportunities may be timed and how categorical exclusions may be managed.

Confirmed facts support a cautious reading. EPA proposed the reforms on June 24, 2026. The Federal Register published draft regulatory amendments on June 25, 2026. The research record does not show final adoption by September 7, 2026. Until the rule is finalized and tested in project reviews, claims about faster permitting are better treated as agency expectations, while claims about lost transparency remain policy risks rather than settled outcomes.

For oversight, the key measure will be the quality of the record left behind: whether affected people can see what was studied, what was excluded, why comments were accepted or rejected and how EPA used its Clean Air Act review authority. A shorter document can still inform the public. A faster process can still be accountable. The unresolved question is whether the proposed procedures will preserve enough public detail for environmental, climate and justice concerns to be evaluated before decisions are made.

description:
India’s solar open access market remains concentrated among a handful of states that have historically dominated installations.
However, Andhra Pradesh, Haryana, Odisha, Punjab, Jharkhand, Telangana, and West Bengal are emerging as markets with varying degrees of untapped potential, according to Mercom’s Q2 and 1H 2026 India Solar Open Access Market Report.
Residential rooftop systems have been driving India’s rooftop solar capacity additions, especially after the introduction of the PM Surya Ghar: Muft Bijli Yojana in 2024.
Vintage View, a residential apartment complex in Thiruvananthapuram, Kerala, has installed a 20 kW rooftop solar system to reduce its electricity bills.
Bangladesh announced a special incentive package to promote rooftop solar systems integrated with battery energy storage.
text:
With a record solar capacity addition of 27 GW in the first half of 2026 and a 110 GWh storage pipeline, India’s clean energy build-out is gathering pace as the country sets its sights on becoming a renewables manufacturing hub. However, the continued reliance on imports for critical solar and battery technologies has raised questions about whether India’s manufacturing growth is being matched by domestic technology development.

India’s solar open access market remains concentrated among a handful of states that have historically dominated installations. However, Andhra Pradesh, Haryana, Odisha, Punjab, Jharkhand, Telangana, and West Bengal are emerging as markets with varying degrees of untapped potential, according to Mercom’s Q2 and 1H 2026 India Solar Open Access Market Report.

Battery energy storage systems (BESS) are evolving from backup power solutions into active energy management assets for commercial and industrial consumers. Peak demand management, tariff optimization, renewable energy integration, diesel generator optimization, and resilience are emerging as potential value streams.

The Central Transmission Utility of India revised the benchmark project costs for solar, wind, and BESS projects used to assess compliance with financial closure and other eligibility requirements for interstate transmission connectivity.

The Uttar Pradesh Electricity Regulatory Commission (UPERC) rejected a petition by a solar manufacturer, seeking unrestricted banking and drawal of power from its proposed captive solar project and 100% exemptions from banking, wheeling, and transmission charges.

UPERC extended the approvals and regulatory relaxations granted to Paschimanchal Vidyut Vitran Nigam for an interstate peer-to-peer renewable energy trading pilot until March 31, 2027.

The Gujarat Electricity Regulatory Commission partially allowed a petition seeking an extension to complete the evacuation infrastructure for its 3.25 MW captive solar project in Mahisagar district.

The Madhya Pradesh High Court recently ruled that prior consent from private landowners is not required for laying power transmission lines.

Residential rooftop systems have been driving India’s rooftop solar capacity additions, especially after the introduction of the PM Surya Ghar: Muft Bijli Yojana in 2024. Over 5 million households have benefited from the program so far. Vintage View, a residential apartment complex in Thiruvananthapuram, Kerala, has installed a 20 kW rooftop solar system to reduce its electricity bills.

The Solar Energy Corporation of India invited bids to select developers to set up 700 MW of interstate transmission system-connected solar power projects in Special Economic Zones or areas designated as Export Oriented Units across the country. The last date to submit bids is October 7, 2026. Bids will be opened the following day.

Gujarat Energy Transmission Corporation floated five tenders to invite bids to set up 1.038 MW of rooftop solar systems across 66 kV substations under Gujarat’s Surendranagar Circle. The last date to submit bids is September 11, 2026.

The Airports Authority of India invited bids to commission a 1.6 MW grid-connected ground-mounted solar project at Maharaja Bir Bikram Airport in Agartala, Tripura. The last date to submit bids is September 26, 2026. Bids will be opened on October 1.

The West Bengal State Electricity Distribution Company (WBSEDCL) invited bids to operate and maintain 8.415 MW of grid-connected rooftop solar projects at WBSEDCL and the West Bengal State Electricity Transmission Company buildings for five years. The last date to submit bids is September 28, 2026. Bids will be opened on September 30.

U.S.-based electric vehicle charging solutions company ChargePoint posted revenue of $116.075 million in the second quarter of the fiscal year 2027, up 17.7% year-over-year from $98.59 million, exceeding analysts’ expectations by $10.8 million.

Bangladesh announced a special incentive package to promote rooftop solar systems integrated with battery energy storage. Under the program, eligible consumers will receive BDT10.5 (~$0.086)/kWh for surplus electricity exported to the national grid after meeting their own consumption requirements.

title: Fresh record set for nuclear generation in 2025
description:
The World Nuclear Association report includes an assessment of progress towards the widely-shared ambition - which 38 countries have signed up to - for a tripling of global nuclear energy capacity by 2050.
(Image: WNA) World Nuclear Association Director General Sama Bilbao y León, said: "This is an extraordinary moment for nuclear energy.
Reflecting on another year of record performance, and looking ahead to a future of record ambition, governments are clear: they need much more nuclear energy to address the interconnected challenges of energy security, affordability, competitiveness and climate goals.
That's why the Association has published recommendations that set the path towards tripling global nuclear energy capacity by 2050.
It also highlights that maintaining and extending the existing fleet is the fastest and most cost-effective ways to secure low-carbon electricity.
text:
The World Nuclear Association report includes an assessment of progress towards the widely-shared ambition - which 38 countries have signed up to - for a tripling of global nuclear energy capacity by 2050. It also sets out a series of policy recommendations.

Listen to report author Jonathan Cobb discuss the findings on the WNN podcast

Focusing on the existing fleet, the report notes that there has been a recent increase in construction starts, as shown by the chart below, which shows how it has fluctuated over the past 75 years.

(Image: WNA)

It also finds that the reliability of nuclear energy plants remains high across the global fleet and across the life of reactors, even as individual units age. The average capacity factor was 83.7% in 2025 (a capacity factor of 100% would be if a unit generated electricity 24 hours a day 365 days a year).

The capacity factor rises as the age of reactors passes 50 years (Image: WNA)

Looking ahead at the prospects for new nuclear capacity, the report projects that it could reach 1,457 GWe by 2050 if all national targets and goals are achieved and the existing fleet continues to operate. With current operating capacity being 423 GWe, that projected figure would be 200 GWe more than a tripling of the current levels.

New capacity under construction increased to 82 GWe, with eleven reactors starting construction in 2025. The combined total of planned, proposed and potential capacity increased to 416 GWe, reducing the gap between actual projects and government targets, although around 550 GW of proposed capacity by 2050 has yet to be translated into specific projects.

(Image: WNA)

As to where the new capacity would be located, the report found that the largest share of the new capacity would come from the established users of nuclear energy - the USA, China, France, Russia and India.

(Image: WNA)

World Nuclear Association Director General Sama Bilbao y León, said: "This is an extraordinary moment for nuclear energy. Reflecting on another year of record performance, and looking ahead to a future of record ambition, governments are clear: they need much more nuclear energy to address the interconnected challenges of energy security, affordability, competitiveness and climate goals.

"But ambition alone will not deliver 24/7 clean energy. That's why the Association has published recommendations that set the path towards tripling global nuclear energy capacity by 2050. We need to make full use of the existing fleet, complete reactors already under construction, capitalising on the acquired capabilities, commit to the next projects and move from individual projects to sustained programmes of deployment."

As well as reviewing the progress towards individual countries' targets, the report includes a series of policy recommendations for governments, industry, financiers and regulators.

These range from "establishing durable policy and investment frameworks, streamlining regulation and strengthening supply chains, to building the workforce, supporting proven reactor deployment and creating the programme-based delivery models needed". It also highlights that maintaining and extending the existing fleet is the fastest and most cost-effective ways to secure low-carbon electricity.

According to World Nuclear Association, "For the rest of this decade, the focus must be on turning national ambitions into credible project pipelines, supported by the institutions, investment, people and industrial capacity needed to deliver them."

text:
DUBAI, 7th September, 2026 (WAM) -- The Water, Energy, Technology and Environment Exhibition (WETEX 2026) will showcase sustainable mobility solutions spanning vehicles, clean energy, charging infrastructure and fleet management from 20th to 22nd October 2026 at the Dubai World Trade Centre.

Organised by Dubai Electricity and Water Authority (DEWA), the exhibition's Green Mobility Zone will bring together electric and hydrogen vehicles, charging technologies and fleet management solutions, connecting transport operators, utilities, investors and technology providers.

The exhibition comes amid accelerating global demand for electric vehicles (EVs). According to the International Energy Agency's (IEA) Global EV Outlook 2026, sales grew by 20 percent to exceed 20 million in 2025, accounting for one quarter of new cars sold. Sales are projected to reach 23 million in 2026, or 28 percent of total car sales.

Saeed Mohammed Al Tayer, MD and CEO of DEWA and Founder and Chairman of WETEX, said, "The future of sustainable mobility requires building an integrated ecosystem that combines clean energy, advanced infrastructure, innovative digital technologies, and business and investment models capable of accelerating the transition to a low-emission green economy."

He stressed the need for reliable charging and power supply solutions, alongside stronger collaboration among governments, companies, research institutions and investors. WETEX supports this transition by facilitating partnerships, knowledge exchange and the adoption of technologies for sustainable cities.

Charging infrastructure remains central to EV growth, with priorities extending beyond charger numbers to charging speed, station distribution, load management and fleet requirements. The IEA reported that public charging points worldwide exceeded seven million at the end of 2025, up by more than 33 percent annually.

Dubai's EV charging points reached 2,223 in the first quarter of 2026. The emirate had 47,944 EVs at the end of 2025, compared with 37,486 a year earlier, an increase of nearly 28 percent.

Vehicle-to-grid (V2G) technology also enables compatible EVs to return stored electricity to the grid, supporting load management and renewable energy integration. Wider adoption depends on vehicle compatibility, standards, regulation and viable business models.

Public and commercial fleets are helping advance electric mobility, with regular routes and high utilisation allowing operators to assess costs and infrastructure efficiency.

DEWA and Dubai Taxi Company (DTC) inaugurated the first phase of an ultra-fast charging hub comprising 24 charging points, each with a capacity of 360 kilowatts (kW). The hub can charge 24 vehicles simultaneously in about 35 minutes.

The initiative forms part of an agreement signed at WETEX 2025 to deploy more than 200 ultra-fast charging points for DTC's fleet. Dubai's Roads and Transport Authority (RTA) also aims to transition its entire public bus fleet to electric and hydrogen power by 2050.

Hydrogen offers a complementary option for heavy-duty, long-haul and high-utilisation transport, where refuelling speed and powertrain weight are significant considerations. The IEA identifies heavy-duty road transport as one of the fastest-growing fuel cell vehicle markets.

DEWA's Green Hydrogen project at the Mohammed bin Rashid Al Maktoum Solar Park is the first in the Middle East and North Africa to produce hydrogen using solar energy. Designed to explore future applications, including transport, the project supplies some of its production to refuel hydrogen vehicles at an ENOC station in Expo City Dubai.

WETEX 2026 will highlight how these technologies can work together to reduce emissions, improve energy efficiency and support sustainable urban transport.

title: Spotting new opportunities in the solar value chain - PV Tech
description:
Mapping the solar value chain For the solar industry, MAPPES.io provides a detailed visualisation of how products connect throughout the manufacturing ecosystem.
“Polysilicon converts to silicon ingot, ingot becomes silicon wafer, silicon wafer becomes solar cell,” Singhal demonstrates, walking PV Tech through the platform’s interactive value chain visualisation.
For each product, MAPPES.io compiles global manufacturer lists that can be sorted by country, capacity and other parameters.
If I click on silicon wafer, then as a solar cell manufacturer, you can think about who the different manufacturers of silicon wafer are.
By mapping the value chain, MAPPES.io revealed how crude oil converts to light naphtha, then to ethylene, which produces ethylene tar as a byproduct.
text:
The traditional methods of discovery—Google searches, personal networks, and annual trade shows—were proving inadequate. “Google will only give you that information which you are searching for, not anything else apart from that,” Singhal says. More troublingly, many Indian companies remained unaware of technologies that had existed for 40 years, “especially those technologies which were not directly in their domain but are relevant to them from a different domain”.

A different approach to industrial intelligence

The solution Singhal envisioned was a platform where information would be funnelled to users rather than requiring them to hunt for it. “We came up with this idea of MAPPES, where you would come to a platform and search for your own technology. Let’s say you make solar cells. You just search for ‘solar cell’, and you follow solar cell, and that’s it. Now, anytime a new supplier, customer, raw material or application gets added in this value chain, you get a notification.”

MAPPES—which stands for Mapping Product Ecosystem—launched in 2017, though Singhal had begun manually mapping products 13 years ago. “It started like that. So we started 13 years ago. And that’s exactly how we started. I was actually sitting in my pyjamas at night, just mapping every product manually, one by one.”

Today, the platform combines a comprehensive product map with a social network overlay, creating what Singhal describes as “a social network around high-technology products”. The key differentiation from platforms like LinkedIn, he explains, is that whereas when you post anything on LinkedIn, it goes into your personal or professional network, on MAPPES.io, it goes into the product network.

Mapping the solar value chain

For the solar industry, MAPPES.io provides a detailed visualisation of how products connect throughout the manufacturing ecosystem. The platform maps the complete journey from polysilicon through to end applications, including byproducts and alternative pathways. “Polysilicon converts to silicon ingot, ingot becomes silicon wafer, silicon wafer becomes solar cell,” Singhal demonstrates, walking PV Tech through the platform’s interactive value chain visualisation. “Solar cells will become modules, and then modules will go into power plants, and then power plants will then power green hydrogen. Green hydrogen will again be used to make polysilicon. So you come back to where it started.”

The platform also captures the complexity of byproducts and alternative applications. Silicon wafer, for instance, can branch into the semiconductor industry for integrated chips, while silicon kerf—the waste generated when cutting ingots into wafers—has its own lifecycle, potentially being converted into silicon metal or silicon-carbon composite anodes for lithium-ion batteries.

For each product, MAPPES.io compiles global manufacturer lists that can be sorted by country, capacity and other parameters. Users can access company pages featuring automatically scraped news, current and announced production capacities, and contact information for personnel who have joined the platform.

Application to the US supply chain

The platform’s value becomes particularly apparent when examining rapidly developing markets like the United States, where policy drivers, including Section 232 tariffs and various anti-dumping duties, are reshaping the PV manufacturing landscape.

“The way I see what’s happening in the US, some of it has already happened in India,” Singhal says, drawing parallels between the two markets. India began by building solar panel manufacturing, then cells, then wafers and ingots. “So all of that is now starting to build up in the US as well.”

However, Singhal identifies a critical blind spot in how the industry typically approaches supply chain development. “Most of the time, the community – and that’s true for any industry, but let’s say the solar community – generally only talks about five products, six products,” he observes. The focus remains on the main value chain—polysilicon, ingot, wafer, cell, module—while overlooking “all the adjacent products that are needed to support the solar ecosystem”.

This oversight creates bottlenecks. “What that means is there are bottlenecks which will come within a year once these manufacturing plants are established. And we are seeing that in India as well. And the same will hold for America,” Singhal says.

Taking silicon ingot production as an example, Singhal explains that crystal growth furnaces require isostatic graphite parts, quartz crucibles and argon gas. “These are the products that will need to be localised very soon, because again, you can’t rely or depend on some other country. In this case, let’s say China, because they are one of the biggest suppliers of ingot pullers and also the isostatic graphite parts.” The platform helps identify these gaps and opportunities. “There will be big manufacturers like the Teslas and the Reliances of the world who will be making the bigger products like the ingots and the wafers and the cells and the panels, but then there are all the other companies, the small and medium scale companies, who are figuring out how to enter this solar ecosystem. What value can they bring?”

Multiple use cases

MAPPES.io serves different functions for different users within an organisation. “Every company on a platform is both a buyer and a seller,” Singhal notes, unlike traditional listing sites such as Alibaba or ThomasNet.

Business development teams can identify potential customers by application. Procurement teams can find raw materials, equipment, and suppliers. Strategy teams can conduct portfolio gap analysis, exploring what additional products they might manufacture. “If you are making solar cells, you’re like, hey, what is something else that I can manufacture? And it could be silicon wafers for that matter, or it could be solar modules.”

“Let’s say I search for silicon wafer. If I click on silicon wafer, then as a solar cell manufacturer, you can think about who the different manufacturers of silicon wafer are. Who are the potential customers for silicon wafer? What does it take to make silicon wafer? What are the raw materials? Who are the suppliers? What machinery? What are the different applications?” Singhal explains.

“And you can basically create a use case to present to your management team that, hey, we should make silicon wafer because this is the kind of competition there is. This is the kind of market out there. We already know the ecosystem, who the suppliers are. These are the applications.”

The platform also reveals connections between seemingly separate industries. Singhal shares an example involving Reliance Industries, which has expanded from oil and petrochemicals into solar, carbon fibre, green hydrogen and batteries. By mapping the value chain, MAPPES.io revealed how crude oil converts to light naphtha, then to ethylene, which produces ethylene tar as a byproduct. This tar can be converted into petroleum coumarone resin, which then becomes either anode coating pitch (used for graphite anodes in lithium-ion batteries) or isotropic pitch-based carbon fibre (used in rigid insulation felts for silicon ingot pullers).

“So if I am Reliance or if I’m looking to partner or sell to Reliance, I would want to understand this value chain,” Singhal explains. “All of a sudden, you can see how this value chain becomes important.” For investors, the platform provides crucial context. “Investors don’t understand manufacturing space as much, right? So they are all seeking to invest in solar and semiconductor, but they don’t know which company to invest in, what does the market look like. They only know what the company will tell them.”

Future development

MAPPES.io is developing an AI agent interface that Singhal hopes to present at the upcoming PV CellTech conference in San Francisco. “You don’t have to go and search for this information. You can just talk to our AI tool and ask who’s the supplier,” he explains. The agent will draw on the platform’s intelligence while filtering out AI hallucinations through its verified product network.

Looking further ahead, carbon footprint mapping represents another potential feature. “For every product, if you know what materials are used, what machinery you use, if you know the carbon footprint of that product, in the future, you’ll be selecting the supplier based on their carbon footprint,” Singhal says. The platform may also evolve to offer more granular information on specific PV technologies such as TOPCon, though this depends on user contributions. “The information [on MAPPES.io] is generated by the ecosystem, not by us,” Singhal emphasises. As users post more detailed technical content, the platform’s AI layer can decode research papers and other materials to create increasingly detailed maps.

A tool for rapid growth

MAPPES.io operates on a freemium model, with basic access available for free and full access requiring an annual membership of around US$3,000. The platform currently covers not just solar but also semiconductors, green hydrogen, lithium-ion batteries, carbon fibre and optical fibre—reflecting Singhal’s insight that “every industry is correlated somehow. At least they are one or two steps away from every other industry out there.”

As the global PV manufacturing industry experiences unprecedented growth, particularly in markets like the United States, where domestic supply chains are being rapidly established, tools that can map complex ecosystems and identify opportunities and bottlenecks before they emerge become increasingly valuable. MAPPES.io offers a way to see not just the obvious connections in the solar value chain, but the hidden links that could determine competitive advantage in an industry racing to scale.

text:
Taipei, Sept. 7 (CNA) Taiwan-based manufacturing giant Hon Hai Precision Industry Co. said it has established a goal of pushing for 100 percent use of green electricity at its production sites around the world by 2040.

In its latest annual sustainability report released Monday, Young Liu (劉揚偉), chairman of the iPhone assembler and AI server maker, said the company will continue to advance energy conservation and carbon reduction, renewable energy, green manufacturing, and the circular economy.

Hon Hai, also known as Foxconn globally, has steadily progressed toward its goals of 100 percent green power use at its plants around the globe by 2040 and net-zero emissions across the value chain by 2050, Liu said in the report.

"We regard the natural environment as important capital for the enterprise's long-term development, and we continue to invest in water resource management, waste circularity, biodiversity, and nature conservation, so that corporate growth and the environment form a positive cycle," Liu added.

According to Hon Hai, green power accounted for 68.37 percent of the company's total power consumption worldwide in 2025, ahead of its original goal of 50 percent by 2030, by taking advantage of Hon Hai's policies in large green power procurement and the introduction of renewable energy into production processes.

In 2025, Hon Hai noted that the company directly procured 1,870.28 GWh of green electricity, while it also procured 4,849.15 GWh of renewable electricity through power trading arrangements to obtain the corresponding green electricity certificates.

Hon Hai said it has adopted a green energy diversification policy to enhance energy supply resilience and electricity use efficiency through clean technologies.

In terms of solar energy projects, Hon Hai added that major plant sites such as those in Taiwan, Vietnam, and Wuhan, Chengdu, Yantai, and Zhengzhou in China, have a combined installed and planned capacity of about 125.68 MW, with an estimated annual power generation of about 117 million kWh.

In terms of its supply chain, Hon Hai said as of the end of 2025, it had required 56 of its suppliers to sign emissions reduction agreements through the "Supplier ESG Digital Management Platform" and to commit to 100 percent green power when rolling out products for Hon Hai, which was ahead of its previous goal of 45 suppliers.

Hon Hai said its target is to require 150 of its suppliers to commit to using 100 percent green power in production for Hon Hai by 2030.

According to the company, it has also continued to expand its efforts to develop clean technologies and services.

In 2025, revenue generated from products and services classified as clean technologies at the company's cloud service subsidiary Foxconn Industrial Internet (FII) accounted for 76.53 percent of the unit's total sales, with cloud computing and high-efficiency data center solutions making up 66.75 percent of the unit's total revenue.

title: Editor's note: the cost of failing to connect climate and clean air - Sustainable Views

text:
Tackling climate change and air pollution together would bring greater economic benefits and raise capital more easily than dealing with them as separate problems, finds a report published this morning.

It is important to spell things out for policymakers, but having spent the weekend reading Elizabeth Gaskell’s North and South, where the negative impacts of industrialisation on health and the environment are impossible to ignore, I do wonder why it has taken the best part of 170 years for such benefits to be costed out.

On their arrival in Milton (aka Manchester) from their genteel home in the south of England, the Hales are horrified by how “outside a thick fog crept up to the very windows, and was driven in to every open door in choking white wreaths of unwholesome mist”.

When mill owner Mr Thornton is introduced to the ladies of the family, Mrs Hale insists on Milton as a “smokey, dirty town”. Thornton suggests things are better than they were, telling Mrs Hale legislation requires furnaces to burn smoke before it is discharged into the city’s air and that he has already implemented such changes as it “repays me in the saving of coal”.

Gaskell may not have directly dealt with climate change — though shortly after she published her novel in the 1850s, another woman, the American Eunice Newton Foote, published a paper linking more carbon dioxide in the atmosphere with a warming world — but the relationship between factory smoke, ill health and the economic savings of reducing pollution are all there.

The UN Environment Programme and the Climate and Clean Air Coalition report concludes every $1 invested in tackling climate change and air pollution together can generate around $15 in economic benefits. It estimates the annual economic benefit of implementing 25 actions dealing with both issues jointly as equivalent to 2.8 per cent of global GDP in 2035, 4.5 per cent in 2050 and 11.4 per cent by 2100. Every year of delayed action would forgo more than $1.5tn annually, the equivalent of 0.5 per cent of GDP, in combined market and non-market benefits, says the report.

“Finance ministries and investors who keep climate and air quality in separate budget lines are leaving trillions on the table,” says the independent co-chair of the assessment, Elliott Harris. Whether the report will trigger a change in thinking and help break down such silos, provoking, in the words of UNEP’s executive director Inger Andersen “decisive leadership from governments, financial institutions and businesses” is an open question. But we can hope it won’t take another 170 years or so before “unparliamentary smoke” — from all sources everywhere — disappears.

In 2025, exposure to human-caused outdoor air pollution was linked to an estimated 6.4mn premature deaths worldwide and found to have contributed to 5.5mn new cases of childhood asthma, 2mn new cases of dementia and millions of heart attacks, cases of pulmonary disease, diabetes, stroke and lung cancer.

Household air pollution, meanwhile, was linked to a further 2mn premature deaths, including around 300,000 children. As the UNEP report factors in, these losses are not just human but also economic in terms of lost productivity.

Women are a key focus of Gaskell’s novels. She makes clear the responsibility of factory pollution in the death of Mrs Hale, for example. And globally women today are more impacted by climate change and air pollution than men, in particular in poorer countries.

Trump pushes US corporate demands in the EU

Elsewhere, Elizabeth keeps the focus on attempts by the US to influence EU sustainability laws. She reports on how the Trump administration’s demands on the EU Corporate Sustainability Due Diligence Directive echo the corporate lobbying campaign led by fossil fuel giants such as ExxonMobil and Chevron.

“Exxon and Chevron indicated very early that they are unhappy with the omnibus compromise, and we know they have good access [to the US government],” says Copenhagen Business School professor and associate dean Andreas Rasche. “[Their lobbying] has been remarkably successful — these companies are very well organised. And the opportunity is now because the Trump administration is open to these debates.”

You can read the full story here.

Three things we are keeping an eye on today:

The Trump administration has proposed amendments to the Clean Water Act, which activists say would weaken its protections. The Environmental Protection Agency has proposed “eliminating federal safeguards for nearly all our nation’s freshwater wetlands and millions of miles of streams” which would be “devastating”, the League of Conservation Voters said.

The state of California is suing Amazon over its treatment of advertisers that use its platforms. Attorney-general Rob Bonta’s suit claims the company misrepresents how it calculates the cost of advertising for more than one million business customers, which he says amounts to deceptive conduct.

California has secured a preliminary injunction in its lawsuit against the Environmental Protection Agency, over the federal regulator’s attempt to block the state’s emissions standards. California was granted waivers under the Clean Air Act to implement stronger emissions limits. The EPA must now withdraw or correct its reclassifications of the waivers.

Until tomorrow,

Philippa

Philippa Nuttall is the editor of Sustainable Views

BEIJING, Sept 7 (Reuters) – China, the world’s largest manufacturer of batteries for energy storage, has temporarily suspended approvals for new ​factories, Chinese financial news outlet Cailianshe ‌reported on Saturday.

• The pause comes as authorities conduct a review of existing and planned energy storage production capacity, with a focus on battery cells, the ‌report ​said, citing industry sources.

• ⁠The move comes amid ⁠growing concerns about overcapacity risks in the energy storage sector, according to the report. That is despite a surge in demand ​for batteries used to balance grids and provide backup power.

• Projects that have not ⁠broken ground will not ⁠move forward for the moment but ​those already under construction will not be affected, ​Cailianshe sources said, adding the policy could ‌be adjusted later.

• China’s energy storage industry has expanded rapidly alongside the country’s renewable energy build-out but, as with other industries like solar ⁠panels and electric vehicle manufacturing, manufacturers have faced mounting pressure from intense competition and falling prices.

• China’s ⁠leading solar ‌manufacturers have also expanded aggressively ⁠into battery energy storage as shrinking ​profits ‌and overcapacity in the panel ​sector push ⁠them to seek new growth opportunities.

• China has taken other steps to rationalise the market including levying a consumption tax on lithium-ion batteries and solar cells.

title: Detroit's Fix for the EV Nobody Bought Weighs 3.75 Tons - Business Model Analyst
description:

text:
Extended-range EVs solve range anxiety by carrying a battery, an engine and a generator at once. Every powertrain shift before this one took parts out.

Stellantis will soon sell you a pickup with a 92 kWh battery, a 3.6-liter Pentastar V-6, an onboard generator, two electric motors and 690 miles of range. It weighs 7,507 pounds empty. It is classified as a half-ton truck.

The Ram 1500 REV is the opening act in what the Wall Street Journal reported on September 6 is the industry’s newest answer to slow EV sales: the extended-range electric vehicle, or EREV. A Jeep Grand Wagoneer version lands first, later this year or early next. Hyundai will put one under the next Santa Fe in 2027, good for roughly 600 miles, with a Genesis variant to follow. Ford, which killed the electric F-150 Lightning last December inside a $19.5 billion restructuring, says the Lightning returns as an EREV.

The trade press is covering this as an engineering fix for range anxiety. Read the bill of materials instead. For fifteen years the case for electrification was subtraction: no transmission, no exhaust, no fuel system, a fraction of the moving parts. The EREV keeps the battery and puts nearly all of it back.

A Half-Ton Truck That Weighs Three and Three-Quarter Tons

Here is the full list of what an extended-range EV deletes compared with a plug-in hybrid: the mechanical connection between engine and wheels, and with it the transmission. That is the deletion. Everything else is addition. The engine stays. The fuel tank, exhaust and emissions hardware stay. A generator gets added. The battery shrinks somewhat versus a full EV but stays large, because these vehicles are being sold on 100-plus miles of electric range.

The Ram 1500 REV comes in 2,671 pounds heavier than a base gas Ram 1500 and 614 pounds heavier than the heaviest F-150 Lightning Ford ever built, which is the truck Ford cancelled for losing money. The compromise product is the heaviest thing in the segment.

Weight is a proxy for cost, and the industry is not hiding it. Analysts and engineers quoted by the Journal expect EREVs to cost more than comparable gas vehicles and possibly more than full EVs. Which is a strange place to land, because the two things that kept Americans out of EVs were price and range. The EREV attacks the second by making the first worse.

Dan Nicholson, a former General Motors vice president, put the whole business case in one sentence: “Customers won’t reject them, but will they pay you extra for it?”

There is a detail in the naming that tells you how fluid the conviction is here. In September 2025, Stellantis cancelled the battery-electric Ram 1500 REV and transplanted the name onto the gas-generator truck previously called the Ramcharger, on the reasoning that REV had better recognition. REV stood for Revolution Electric Vehicle. It is now the badge on a truck with a V-6 under the hood.

Ford Is Funding Two Opposite Diagnoses at Once

Watch what Ford is doing, because it is running both answers simultaneously and only one of them can be right.

Diagnosis one: EVs failed on price. That is Ford’s own stated read. Jim Farley’s explanation in December 2025 was that every American EV flop was a $50,000-plus product. The response is the Fathom, a $28,350 electric pickup ($29,945 delivered) built on a Universal EV Production System with roughly 20 percent fewer parts and up to 40 percent faster assembly. Ford gutted Louisville Assembly to build it and wants more than 100,000 units in year one. That bet is entirely about stripping content out.

Diagnosis two: EVs failed on range. The response is an EREV Lightning, which adds content back, adds weight, and lands at a higher price than the truck it replaces.

Ford is capitalizing both. The company already runs two businesses with opposite customer economics inside one P&L, so this is in character. But price and range are competing explanations for the same failure, and hedging across both costs real engineering money at a company that just took $19.5 billion of charges to buy back flexibility it had spent away.

Note what is absent from all of this. Nobody is being paid to build EREVs in the United States. The $7,500 consumer credit expired in September 2025. The CAFE civil penalty was reset to zero by statute in July 2025, which is why the Hemi came back and why nothing in this fleet math is subsidized. In China, where the format was commercialized, EREVs qualify as new energy vehicles and earn credit treatment. In America they earn nothing. The entire case rests on a customer voluntarily paying more for redundancy.

Where the Engineering Actually Wins

The steelman is stronger than the skeptics admit.

For a 7,000-pound vehicle, kilowatt-hours are a lousy way to buy range. Batteries scale badly with mass, cost and charge time, and towing eviscerates EV range in a way that a gasoline generator simply does not notice. That is the specific failure mode that sank the F-150 Lightning and the Silverado EV with truck buyers. Three-row SUVs have the same problem: enormous packs, punishing recharge windows, a use case built around long trips.

The comparison to failed plug-in hybrids also flatters the EREVs. Those cars were gas vehicles with a token battery. The Subaru Crosstrek plug-in offered 17 all-electric miles. The plug-in Wrangler managed about 20. Even the Chevrolet Volt, the best of them, topped out near 50. The Ram 1500 REV claims 145 miles of electric range, which means most owners genuinely would rarely burn fuel. That is a different product, not a rerun.

And the format works at scale somewhere. Li Auto built its company on extended-range SUVs in China and passed 1,801,834 cumulative deliveries at the end of August 2026.

Three things cut the other way. Plug-in hybrids never exceeded one or two percent of the US new-car market, and plenty of owners never plugged them in at all, which is a base rate no amount of engineering elegance overrides. Li Auto is now building battery-electric platforms in parallel, so the company that proved EREVs is diversifying out of them at the exact moment Detroit diversifies in. And the Ram itself has been promised since 2023 with launch dates of late 2024, then 2025, then the first quarter of 2026, and now a 2027 model year. Four slips before a single customer delivery is its own kind of data.

The Business Model Angle

Content per vehicle is the actual trade being made. The EV thesis was supposed to compress the supplier base by deleting the engine, transmission, exhaust and fuel system. EREVs reverse it. Powertrain suppliers, inverter and generator makers, thermal management specialists and engine plants that were on a closure list all get a reprieve, and the vehicle’s parts count goes up rather than down. If you were positioned for the subtraction, you were positioned wrong.

The hedge is being sold as the product. Automakers are moving optionality off the balance sheet and into the vehicle, then invoicing the customer for it. That playbook is repeatable anywhere a transition is genuinely uncertain: dual-fuel industrial boilers, dual-sourced compute, grid assets built to run on two inputs. The open question is universal. People say they value optionality. They rarely pay a visible premium for redundancy they expect never to use.

Dealer fixed operations come back, and so does the warranty tail. This one is a take, not a reported figure. Battery-electric vehicles gut service revenue, which is where franchised dealers make their margin. An EREV restores oil changes, filters, plugs, coolant loops and emissions hardware while adding the entire EV stack on top. Dealers get their annuity back. Manufacturers inherit two warranty exposures in one vehicle.

The Takeaway

The industry spent fifteen years arguing that electric cars would win because they were simpler. When that argument stalled at the showroom, the compromise it produced is not simpler than either thing it replaces. It is a 7,507-pound pickup that carries two complete ways of moving itself and asks the buyer to fund both. Detroit gets its answer at the configurator, and the badge on the door will say Revolution.

text:
It’s Monday, and that’s when we like to take a look at current business issues that are trending across our state and discuss them with one of our fellow news media friends. This week, Mike Switzer interviews Jessica Holdman, a reporter with the South Carolina Daily Gazette in Columbia, SC. Jessica tells us about a Spartanburg data center creating its own power but much more than originally projected. She also tells us about Duke Energy asking the SC Supreme Court to overturn the Public Service Commission’s ruling that Duke must wait a year before raising rates. And finally she updates us on the status of the $150 million needed to pay for cost overruns at the Scout Motors site in Blythewood, SC.

TRANSCRIPT:

Switzer: Hello and welcome to the South Carolina Business Review. This is Mike Switzer. It's Monday and that's when we like to take a look at current business issues that are trending across our state and discuss them with one of our fellow news media friends. This week we have Jessica Holdman, a reporter with the South Carolina Daily Gazette, a non profit news agency. And she joins us by phone now from her office in Columbia. Jessica, welcome back to the program.

Holdman: Thanks, Mike.

Switzer: So tell us what's showing up on your radar this week.

Holdman: Well, Mike, we've got a few headlines in the utility and power generation sphere going on. I think you and I have probably talked before about a data center in Spartanburg County. this one's being developed by Northmark Strategies and what they want to do is they want to make their own power. Now we've heard the argument against data centers that they take so much energy and it's showing up on power customers bills. Well, this company wanted to avoid that by producing their own power, but they've seen some challenges. There's been some environmental and citizens groups that are worried about air pollution from the generators they would use to do this. In this past week or so, the Public Service Commission said that actually the company's not subject to the same regulatory process as power plants are in the state. They can just go through the environmental review process.

Switzer: I guess they're not considering clean energy.

Holdman: Right. So this would be a natural gas fired turbines. Really big concern that the environmental groups raised is that when they came in they were saying, oh, we just need 50 megawatts. Then they came back and said actually it's going to be more than that. They actually upped that to needing 450 megawatts worth of generators on site. So drastic change in the amount of energy being produced certainly is. All right.

Switzer: You mentioned more in the electric, utility, sector.

Holdman: Absolutely. Duke Energy was the first utility in the state to opt to use a new mechanism that legislators passed here couple legislative sessions ago and that was setting up a process where utility companies could raise their rates on an annual basis without having to go through the full blown regulatory process. They do still have to make their argument before regulators, but it's not as long and drawn out. And when they went before the Public Service Commission, the commissioner said, well, you can do this but you're going to have to wait. They wanted the utility to have essentially a base year before they could go in and ask for a rate increase. Duke Energy is, saying that's not the way that the law was written, so they're asking the Supreme Court to step in.

Switzer: Okay, so do we know when that decision might come down?

Holdman: Well, that's really hard to say. When the court decides to take up that case remains to be seen.

Switzer: All right, Jessica, we have time for one more. What else have you found?

Holdman: One other thing we've talked about on the show in the past, Mike, is the cost overruns at the Scout Motors plant. There were some questions about whether the state would step in and cover those overruns. There was some money put in the budget with the stipulation that the money couldn't be paid out until a full blown investigation had taken place. Governor in his veto powers, stepped in and said, you know, you can have this study conducted, but we don't need to be waiting to cut that check. Most of those cost overruns were tied to environmental remediation, fixing wetlands to make up for those that were lost when the site was leveled.

Switzer: All right, so I guess this $150 million, now it's paid and the, controversy over that with Scout Motors is over.

Holdman: yeah, I mean, I'm sure we'll still see that investigation into how we got there go forward, but the question of will they or won't they has been answered.

Switzer: Well, Jessica, thank you so much for the update.

Holdman: Thanks, Mike.

Switzer: Jessica Holdman is a reporter with the South Carolina Daily Gazette. She spoke to us by phone from her office in Columbia. We will have a link to the nonprofit news source in our state posted at our webpage so you can learn more south Carolina public radio.org or you can hear this show again. And you can hear us again wherever you find podcasts with the South Carolina Business Review. This is Mike Switzer.

text:
AYESHA RASCOE, HOST:

The public backlash to data centers is moving so fast that politicians have been rushing to keep up. In Pennsylvania, Democratic Governor Josh Shapiro is running for reelection. Both he and Stacy Garrity, his Republican opponent, have been trying to respond to this backlash. Kat Bolus from member station WVIA in Pittston, Pennsylvania, has this report.

KAT BOLUS, BYLINE: Just over a year ago, Governor Josh Shapiro touted the investment of some $20 billion by Amazon to build data centers in the state.

(SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED RECORDING)

JOSH SHAPIRO: For too long, we've watched as towns across Pennsylvania got hollowed out and left behind. No more. Now is our time to rebuild those communities and invest in them.

BOLUS: The next day, State Treasurer Stacy Garrity celebrated the Amazon investment. She posted on X, it will create thousands of jobs for Pennsylvanians. She's running against Shapiro now. On Talk Radio 1210 WPHT in Philadelphia, she mentioned areas of rural Pennsylvania and said...

(SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED RECORDING)

STACY GARRITY: What perfect places to put data centers.

BOLUS: That was last year. Now around 100 data centers are proposed across the state. Pennsylvanians packed meeting halls to demand their lawmakers slow down the industry. And in the governor's race, Garrity has now called for a pause on data centers.

(SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED RECORDING)

GARRITY: A pause doesn't mean you have to pause for a year. A pause means you have to pause to make sure that you get it right to make sure that there's balance.

BOLUS: As for Shapiro, he's called for new data center regulations. In May, he was in Archbald, Pennsylvania, where several data centers are being considered.

(SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED RECORDING)

SHAPIRO: It is clear to me that there are real concerns in the communities all across Pennsylvania, especially here in Archbald. And I want you to know that I have real concerns as well.

BOLUS: Last month, he signed an executive order requiring data center companies to be more transparent, pay for their energy needs and protect the environment. And he referred back to that Amazon deal that he said would rebuild communities.

(SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED RECORDING)

SHAPIRO: Since then, we have seen an unacceptable number of speculative proposals for data center development that is swamping our commonwealth, many of them led by developers who have no regard for local communities.

BOLUS: Chris Borick is a political science professor at Lehigh University in Bethlehem, Pennsylvania.

CHRIS BORICK: And what happened, I think, to not only Garrity and Shapiro, but almost any elected official, was that they were caught off guard in some ways by the speed and intensity of the shift in public attitudes.

BOLUS: Across the country, from Democrat Kathy Hochul in New York to Texas Republican Greg Abbott, governors have been calling to slow down data center development. Here's Borick again.

BORICK: And you look at almost any polling metric right now in Pennsylvania and beyond, and it's clear that people are not at all enamored with the way the issue's been handled to date. That's a problem for incumbents.

BOLUS: In Pennsylvania, both campaigns have ads claiming their candidate will be tougher on data centers. Meanwhile, town meetings continue across the state with residents speaking out against data centers in their neighborhoods.

For NPR News, I'm Kat Bolus in Pittston, Pennsylvania.

RASCOE: Amazon is a financial supporter of NPR and pays to distribute some of our content. Transcript provided by NPR, Copyright NPR.

Editor’s note: The following is an excerpt from the “Myths and Misconceptions” section of Enemies of Energy, a research report created for the Capital Research Center. The page for the full report is here: Enemies of Energy.

***

In a 2014 interview, billionaire investor Warren Buffett made this observation about federal energy subsidies: [i]

I will do anything that is basically covered by the law to reduce Berkshire’s tax rate. For example, on wind energy, we get a tax credit if we build a lot of wind farms. That’s the only reason to build them. They don’t make sense without the tax credit. [ii]

According to the U.S. Department of Energy, 91 percent of all the energy used in America in 2024 was generated from hydrocarbon and nuclear fuels. We are not unique: Our World in Data reports that more than 85 percent of the planet’s energy consumption comes from these four fuels. [iii] [iv]

During a 14-year stretch from 2010 through 2023, according to an October 2024 report from the Texas Public Policy Foundation, hydrocarbon and nuclear fuels combined received $79 billion in federal energy subsides. [v]

That report also shows a far larger subsidy of $141 billion combined for wind and solar energy development over the era. [vi]

Similarly, in September 2023, energy journalist Robert Bryce compared federal subsidies against the energy produced by each system subsidized for 2022. He found that solar power received 302 times more in tax incentives per British thermal unit (Btu) of energy output than nuclear power, and 136 times more than oil and gas. Wind subsidies were 69 times more than nuclear and 31 times more than oil and gas. [vii]

And all of this is just a partial look at the huge corporate subsidies that have been dedicated to weather dependent energy systems. The federal wind and solar credits for commercial energy developers were first enacted way back 1992.[viii] [ix]

Wind power contributed just 1.6 percent of total American energy in 2024 and solar just 1.2 percent. For comparison, the Department of Energy claims the burning of wood and other biomass was good for 2.3 percent of total energy output.[x] [xi]

So, after more than three decades of outsized federal subsidies that were supposed to turn wind and solar into the fuels of our future, they are still unable to rival the output of an energy option that has existed since we first harnessed fire 400,000 years ago. [xii]

title: Six of the 16 major emitters reduced their emissions in 2025 - Joint Research Centre
description:
Shifting trends among major global emitters The six largest emitters—China, the United States, India, the EU, Russia, and Indonesia—together accounted for 62% of global GHG emissions in 2025.
Six of the 16 major emitters (contributing over 1% of global emissions) achieved reductions in 2025, including Australia, Brazil and Japan.
Additionally, the EU GHG emissions per capita (7.1 t CO2eq/cap) continued their decline towards the global average value (6.6 t CO2eq/cap).
Wildfires generated 2.2 Gt CO₂eq in global emissions in 2025.
Related links European Commission’s Emissions Database for Global Atmospheric Research (EDGAR) JRC report: GHG emissions of all world countries EU GHG Inventory Competitive Compass Clean Industrial Deal International Energy Agency UNFCCC UNEP Emissions Gap Report
text:
Human activities worldwide in 2025 emitted a record 54 gigatonnes (Gt) of CO₂ equivalent (CO₂eq) emissions into the atmosphere, excluding land use, land-use change, and forestry (LULUCF).

This marks a 0.7% rise compared to 2024. Thus, the post-COVID-19 upward trajectory continues, although at a lower rate compared to the previous year, according to the latest data from the European Commission’s Emissions Database for Global Atmospheric Research (EDGAR), compiled in cooperation with the International Energy Agency (IEA) and published in a new JRC report, GHG emissions of all world countries.

Shifting trends among major global emitters

The six largest emitters—China, the United States, India, the EU, Russia, and Indonesia—together accounted for 62% of global GHG emissions in 2025. However, emission changes varied significantly across key economies and sectors:

The United States registered the largest absolute rise worldwide, increasing emissions by +2.2% compared to 2024.

For the first time, China and India maintained or reduced their emission levels (+0.1% and -0.2%).

Reductions were observed across major contributors. Six of the 16 major emitters (contributing over 1% of global emissions) achieved reductions in 2025, including Australia, Brazil and Japan.

The EU reduced its greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions (excluding LULUCF) by 0.2% relative to 2024, achieving a 35.6% total reduction from 1990 levels. The EU's share of global total emissions declined further to 5.8%. Additionally, the EU GHG emissions per capita (7.1 t CO2eq/cap) continued their decline towards the global average value (6.6 t CO2eq/cap). Note that the EDGAR figures have a different basis than those used to track progress towards EU targets, based on the EU GHG Inventory.

Türkiye recorded the highest relative increase among major emitters (+4.2%), alongside notable rises in Iran and Saudi Arabia.

Aviation and maritime shipping continued their post-pandemic rebound, increasing by 5.1% and 1.4%, respectively.

Land use and wildfires

Atmospheric CO₂ can accumulate as carbon in vegetation and soils, which act as sinks. Through the LULUCF sector, human activities directly affect these carbon stores. In 2025, LULUCF was a net source of about 0.9 Gt CO2eq globally, equivalent to 1.6% of global GHG emissions of that year, also due to the contribution of wildfires.

However, carbon removal mechanisms faced severe pressure:

Deforestation released 3.7 Gt CO₂, offsetting more than twice the amount removed by the LULUCF sink globally.

Wildfires generated 2.2 Gt CO₂eq in global emissions in 2025. While this was below the long-term historical average, regional spikes were observed.

The EU LULUCF sector remained a net forest sink at around 0.2 Gt CO₂eq, but carbon removal levels were lower than in 1990, driven in part by increased regional wildfire emissions from 2024 to 2025 (+40%).

Background

Research supporting policies aimed at climate neutrality is a strategic priority for the JRC. EDGAR’s robust, independent scientific data directly feeds into the Competitive Compass and the Clean Industrial Deal—two key EU initiatives focused on enhancing the sustainability, competitiveness, and autonomy of EU industries while helping decision-makers navigate the economic costs of climate action.

Managed by the JRC in cooperation with the International Energy Agency (IEA), EDGAR provides independent, comparable data across all countries and sectors from 1970 to 2025, supporting European Commission policy through the Directorate-General for Climate Action in UN climate negotiations under the UNFCCC.

Additionally, EDGAR data directly feeds into the annual UNEP Emissions Gap Report, the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) Assessment Reports and supports the IPCC Task Force on National Greenhouse Gas Inventories to map global emission hotspots and guide evidence-based mitigation.
