BARCELONA, Spain, Sept. 7, 2026 /PRNewswire/ — Smart City Expo World Congress (SCEWC), the leading international event on cities and smart urban solutions organized by Fira de Barcelona, will hold its 2026 edition from November 3 to 5 at Barcelona’s Gran Via venue, bringing together 1,000 cities, more than 25,000 attendees, over 1,000 exhibitors and 600 speakers. Under the theme “Urban Solutions, Real Impact,” this year’s edition will place special focus on housing, one of the most pressing challenges facing cities worldwide, while showcasing technologies designed to deliver tangible, scalable impact.

The congress program is structured around seven tracks — Enabling Technologies, Energy & Environment, Mobility, Governance & Economy, Living & Inclusion, Infrastructure & Building, and Blue Economy — spanning digital transformation, artificial intelligence, green energy, governance and social equity.

Over 600 experts will take part in the sessions, including Nikolas Badminton, Chief Futurist and Think Tank leader at Futurist.com, who will share his vision on the future of cities. An artificial intelligence expert, Badminton helps companies and institutions build strategic foresight capabilities, identify the trends shaping the world, anticipate unforeseen risks, and prepare for complex, evolving environments through long-term thinking and scenario planning.

Ayumi Moore Aoki, founder of Women in Tech Global, will also participate in the congress. Her work focuses on the importance of diversity and inclusion as key drivers of innovation in the urban context. Moore Aoki underscores how inclusive leadership can support sustainable urban development at scale. The conference also features Bibiana Aido of UN Women, Bilel Jamoussi of the ITU, and Chiara Corazza of the Women’s Economic Forum, among others.

SCEWC will host the first edition of HOWS Barcelona, a new housing world summit that will focus on topics such as urban planning and land policy, housing regulation, social and affordable housing, and building renovation and reuse, opening a debate on the foundations of a new residential paradigm.

The exhibition floor will host global companies including Google, Microsoft, NVIDIA, Dell Technologies and Deutsche Telekom IoT, alongside a wide range of country and city pavilions and the new “Terra50” showcase, unveiling the world’s top 50 sustainability solutions in the urban field.

SCEWC 2026 will run jointly with Tomorrow.Mobility World Congress, Tomorrow.Blue Economy, HOWS Barcelona, Barcelona Deep Tech Summit, and Barcelona Cybersecurity Congress, consolidating Barcelona as a global meeting point for urban innovation this November.

title: The Winners and Losers of Maine's Race to Armor Its Shoreline Against Climate Change
authors: Derek Harrison, Emmett Gartner, Claire Barber
description:

The rule changes respond to years of research demonstrating the collateral damage sea walls and other hard infrastructure can have on neighboring stretches of shoreline.

text:
GORHAM, Maine—Supersonic shockwaves shook the bones of Charlie Hamblen’s historic Maine farmhouse more than a dozen times last year, travelling over half a mile from blasts at a nearby quarry.

The quarry is one of two active in Gorham, a vibrant and growing town of nearly 20,000 residents a few miles west of Portland, and its frequent blasts are emblematic of a broader trend spanning Maine in recent years: The state’s construction aggregate industry is booming, thanks at least in part to climate change, as property owners erect or repair stone walls to protect against sea level rise, flooding and erosion.

The number of permits to develop new quarries have more than tripled in Maine over the past five years compared to the prior decade, according to the Maine Department of Environmental Protection (DEP). Meanwhile, quarry owners in Gorham and beyond are looking to expand their existing pits, potentially bringing more Maine residents into the pathway of the quarries’ shockwaves.

“If they expand this quarry, we figure it’s going to impact at least another 300 existing houses, let alone the new houses being built,” said Hamblen.

The growth in quarries coincides with trends in Maine and elsewhere in New England, including steady increases in construction and recurring annual road maintenance needs, but also the climate-amplified boom in stone walls.

After a trio of destructive winter storms inundated the central Maine foothills and slammed into the coast two years ago—illuminating the state’s vulnerability to similar climate change-fueled storms—the number of permit applications for seawall projects skyrocketed, expedited by an emergency permitting provision in state statute and a slew of federal disaster funds.

“They had a window in there for a while and you were able to just go and do an emergency repair,” said Skip Murray, owner of the family construction company L.P. Murray & Sons on the southern Maine coast. “I did a lot of work in municipalities in that time frame, and then that was still when you could get reimbursed” by the Federal Emergency Management Agency.

According to a rough analysis of state permit data by the Maine DEP, the number of applications for shoreline stabilization permits nearly tripled from 118 in 2022 to 313 in 2024. Department spokesperson David Madore said the state could not precisely differentiate between projects with sea walls and those without, however, he added that “most applications were for riprap stabilization”—the stone slabs and crushed rock that form the walls.

There are few state regulations on quarries in Maine, critics say, and following the recent surge, more and more towns are considering local moratoriums on new quarries, strengthened ordinances that greatly restrict the activity of existing ones, and even local restrictions on new rock sea walls.

Similar clashes among residents, quarry owners and municipal officials are unfolding beyond Gorham as towns contend with this growth and determine how best to plan for climate change and the state’s mineral needs.

A Booming Industry

There are roughly 780 active mining facilities across Maine, each excavating a unique combination of minerals and often refining or processing them on-site into sand, rock, gravel and riprap for a variety of construction purposes.

From 2015 to 2021, the state saw a consistent average of three new quarry registrations per year, according to DEP mining coordinator Michael Clark, which then shot up to roughly 10 per year between 2022 and 2025, not counting a handful of expansions at existing quarries.

Clark said that he can’t be sure what’s specifically driving that trend but thought that riprap demand could be some part of it, whether it’s used for sea walls or other common uses, such as culvert construction.

Data published by the U.S. Geological Survey shows the value of crushed rock, gravel and sand produced at Maine quarries has doubled over that same period—hovering around $100 million in 2021 and a few years prior, then ballooning to more than $220 million last year.

There isn’t accompanying data on the weight or amount of construction material generating that value, but there is evidence that Maine isn’t the only New England state seeing a surge in aggregate activity.

The Massachusetts islands of Nantucket and Martha’s Vineyard have received a 125 percent increase of construction aggregate that’s been barged over the past 10 years as well as a variety of new coastal resilience projects, according to reporting from The New Bedford Light, while sand excavation sites crop up on the mainland.

Most Maine quarries are concentrated away from the coast, in towns like Gorham or Bridgton, and the state doesn’t closely regulate them beyond their pit size, blasts, dust emissions and equipment exhaust. The amount of blasting or rock crushing varies from quarry to quarry and often depends on whether there’s an obstacle of solid bedrock called ledge.

“There’s generally not blasting unless there’s a ledge,” Clark with the DEP said. “So most pits don’t have ledge. I’ve encountered some, but most do not.”

Despite that variety, many quarry neighbors have similar complaints about the quarries that do use explosives or intensive rock crushing. They describe plumes of dust and disruptive blasting operations they suspect are damaging their homes. They also complain about empty promises from quarry contractors who often refuse to share analysis of the blasts’ seismic data from their property lines. Meanwhile, there is limited oversight from municipal officials, the neighbors say.

More Blasting in Gorham?

In Gorham, Charlie Hamblen was motivated to run for town council last year by Gorham’s weak quarry ordinances and an ongoing proposal by local aggregate company Shaw Brothers Construction to expand its Brickyard Quarry near Hamblen’s home. He won the election in November 2025.

“The town was not willing to listen to the [quarry] neighbors and work on ordinances to make it a safer place for people, so I got crazy and I ran for town council,” Hamblen said.

Gorham is one of at least five Maine towns in the past two years that have received proposals for new or expanded quarries or considered adopting new ordinances to regulate them.

The town issued Shaw Brothers a permit for its 6.7-acre quarry back in 2008 that allows for industrial rock crushing and an average of roughly 10 to 11 blasts per year.

Under a permit application submitted last year, the company proposed expanding the quarry to the majority of a 26-acre parcel adjacent to the existing pit and capping the number of blasts at 18 per year.

The Gorham town council rejected it in February 2025, and Shaw Brothers withdrew a subsequent request to rezone the area for industrial development, putting the project partly on hold until the company resubmitted its rezoning request earlier this summer. The Gorham planning board then unanimously recommended that the town council approve the request in early August. Now it is up to councilors to decide.

Hamblen saw the pause as the perfect opportunity for the town to explore amendments to its current mineral extraction ordinance, which has no annual limit on the number of blasts a quarry can execute so long as they meet a set of criteria. The blasts must be approved by the town, and accompanied by detailed blasting reports with seismic data made available for public view.

At the August rezoning meeting, Shaw Brothers owner Dan Shaw told the Gorham planning board that between the town’s ordinances and state regulations, the company is already “regulated to the hilt” and has addressed some environmental concerns by powering quarry operations from the energy provided by a nearby solar farm.

Maine is growing, Shaw argued, and the construction material fueling that development has to come from somewhere.

“We need quarries,” for construction in Maine, Shaw added. “We need concrete. We need hospitals. We need roads.”

Shaw Brothers Construction did not respond to an interview request ahead of publication.

Hamblen and other municipal officials have been looking to the central Maine town of Winthrop for inspiration after it adopted some of the most stringent mineral extraction regulations in the state when confronted with a quarry development application in 2023. Under its updated ordinance, Winthrop now restricts the number of blasts per year, has size-caps on quarry expansion requests and heightened monitoring requirements.

Voters in South Thomaston adopted similar provisions earlier this June in the aftermath of a since-rescinded expansion request from a local quarry, whose owner sits on the town planning board.

As some towns wrap up their responses to new or expanded quarry proposals, either approving restrictive ordinances or denying development permits outright, others are still receiving applications for new pits and starting from the beginning.

Residents in the town of Berwick near the New Hampshire border in southwest Maine are the latest to grapple with a new quarry proposal, this time for a 62-acre sand and gravel pit that would dispatch an average of 20 truckloads of material each day for six days a week.

Meanwhile, just 20 miles north in Alfred, the town planning board rejected a quarry proposal in August from prominent southern Maine construction and excavation company Gorham Sand & Gravel.

Each new proposal catches some towns off-guard and sets others down monthslong deliberations over their comprehensive plans or zoning ordinances.

Stonewalls or Wetlands

Whether this recent uptick in Maine quarries continues could be undercut by converging market forces developing outside of the aggregate industry. Earlier this summer, the Maine Department of Transportation—a massive buyer of construction aggregate of all types—announced it would be dropping up to $400 million in road construction projects after a steep budget shortfall.

Maine’s environmental agency, meanwhile, has since updated its permitting process for shoreline erosion projects to prioritize “nature-based” solutions that use plants or biodegradable materials and adds more stringent requirements for hard infrastructure like sea walls.

The rule changes respond to years of research demonstrating the collateral damage sea walls and other hard infrastructure can have on neighboring stretches of shoreline. That’s because wave energy doesn’t magically dissipate when it thrashes into plates of stone or concrete armor on the shore. Instead, the force ricochets up or down the coast and collides with beaches, bluffs or marshes that absorb the blow instead, hastening erosion in some places.

After the rush of more than 300 sea wall permits following the 2024 winter storms, the number of permits dropped back down to around 190 in 2025—close to levels before the storm.

Craig Coolidge, principal engineer and president of Maine consulting firm Summit Geoengineering, said that could be due to the additional hurdles added by the permitting rule changes, many of which now take up to nine months for approval after historically taking only six.

Since the rule changes went into effect earlier this year, Coolidge’s firm is incorporating more plantings and regenerative sediment that fills in shorelines carved away by erosion. However, he said, those “soft” approaches can’t always meet the engineering demands that armored infrastructure projects can, resulting in continued sea wall construction at a slower permitting pace.

“The vision was good, but the execution is just not there yet,” Coolidge said of the permitting changes.

Sea Wall Begets Sea Wall

Twelve miles up the coast from South Thomaston, voters in the tourist hub of Camden went a step further than the Maine DEP when they approved a 180-day moratorium on all coastal shoreline armoring projects this June in a landslide referendum.

The ban grew out of the proliferation of sea wall projects following the 2024 winter storms, said Camden planning and development coordinator Jeremy Martin, which rocked Camden especially hard due to the town’s high exposure to strong winds and storm surges.

Similar to some municipalities’ lack of quarry ordinances, Camden doesn’t have any codes on the town’s books that guide responsible sea wall development, Martin said, and the ban gives officials time to develop best practices to keep properties safe and protect the shoreline.

The current gap in oversight has led to one especially fortified stretch of riprap on a slope overlooking Sherman Cove, a scenic inlet with deep blue waters just north of Camden’s downtown. Martin said that the sheer amount of stone trucked in to build it wore down the road leading to a public boat launch.

Meanwhile, sea wall begets sea wall, causing a domino effect of Camden residents armoring their shores to protect their properties from the waves sent cascading up or down from their neighbors’ walls, according to Martin. Camden beaches and coastal habitat rely on a stable pattern of erosion to backfill the sand lost from tidal forces, but sea walls can halt erosion altogether—both good and bad.

“It impacts the natural environment, abutting property owners, and public infrastructure, and that’s why I think voters overwhelmingly approved the moratorium ordinance,” Martin said.

Martin said he understands why coastal property owners feel compelled to protect their homes and shorelines. The ordinances he and Camden officials are considering will keep that vulnerability in mind. They are likely to be modelled after another Camden ordinance Martin spearheaded that requires rigorous review for private piers and wharfs to ensure they’re built for longevity and cohesion.

Camden’s goals overlap with those of the towns seeking moratoriums and revised regulations on quarries. Both sets are trying to wrap their arms around statewide trends unspooling in their backyards before new projects are permitted and developed. Otherwise, whether it’s a quarry or sea wall, it will only have to meet the state’s requirements for permitting.

“I think the people here have decided … if there’s going to be a problem or impacts, we need to address them,” Martin said.

The Governor of Massachusetts, Maura Healey, and the Mass Clean Energy Center (MassCEC) have announced USD 4.2 million in funding to 20 projects that will prepare workers for offshore wind and maritime careers, and support research on fisheries, wildlife, and the marine environment.

The funding is awarded through two MassCEC programs: USD 1.7 million through the Offshore Wind Works program and USD 2.4 million through the Offshore Wind Science, Research and Analysis program.

''Offshore wind means good jobs, more clean energy and real economic opportunity for Massachusetts,'' said Governor Healey.

''We’re investing in the workers who will build this industry and the research needed to develop it responsibly and protect our fisheries, wildlife and marine environment.''

Through Offshore Wind Works, USD 1.7 million will support eight projects in building a Massachusetts workforce that is capable of planning, deploying, operating, maintaining, and manufacturing components for offshore wind projects. Many of the skills and credentials developed through these projects are transferable across clean energy, maritime, construction, and other port-based industries—strengthening workforce resilience beyond offshore wind alone. Since launching in 2018, Offshore Wind Works has awarded USD 22 million to 35 grantees, leveraging more than USD 11 million in additional cost-sharing.

''These two efforts work in tandem: one grows the talent pipeline for offshore wind projects, the other expands the knowledge base the industry needs for the long haul,'' said Ben Downing, Mass Clean Energy Center CEO.

''Investing in both is how Massachusetts prepares the way for future accelerated offshore wind deployment.''

This year’s awards will fund projects across three focus areas: Workforce Training & Upskilling; Training Equipment & Infrastructure; and Career Exploration & Education. The projects are expected to leverage an estimated USD 892,241 in additional cost-sharing and in-kind contributions from grantees and their partners.

The 2026 Offshore Wind Works awardees are:

Massachusetts Maritime Academy: USD 260,000 for Workforce Training & Upskilling

Funding will be used to establish the equipment, certifications, and instructional capacity needed to deliver Helicopter Underwater Escape Training.

Partners: RelyOn USA

TITAN Structural Group LLC: USD 500,000 for Workforce Training & Upskilling and Training Equipment & Infrastructure

Funding will be used to equip trades workers with offshore wind safety and technical certifications.

Partners: Ironworkers; IBEW; IUPAT union affiliates

UMass Dartmouth: USD 250,000 for Career Exploration & Education

Funding will be used to add 30 paid internship opportunities to the offshore wind internship program.

UMass Boston: USD 249,243 for Career Exploration & Education

Funding will be used to develop and deliver ten learning modules covering offshore wind topics ranging from engineering and aquaculture to ports and supporting infrastructure.

Partners: Academic Center for Reliability and Resilience of Offshore Wind (ARROW)

STEAM the Streets: USD 209,330 for Career Exploration & Education

Funding will be used to launch a statewide campaign to increase public understanding of offshore wind and clean energy careers.

Partners: Environmental League of Massachusetts; Boston Public Schools; New Bedford Public Schools; MassHire South Shore; MassHire Greater New Bedford

UMass Amherst: USD 141,427 for Career Exploration & Education

Funding will be used to expand the Career Access Scholarship Program, enhance workforce training with a focus on transferable skills, and foster new partnerships between Massachusetts and Nova Scotia.

Partners: MANSA Consulting; Salem Alliance for the Environment; Spirit Advisory

MANSA Consulting, Inc: USD 100,000 for Career Exploration & Education

Funding will be used to expand the WindWorks campaign to increase awareness of offshore wind career opportunities and connect participants to introductory offshore wind training.

Partners: Bristol Community College; IWNL Energy

Trustees of Tufts University: USD 40,000 for Career Exploration & Education

Funding will be used to publish findings on offshore wind workers' experiences, safety culture, and working conditions, while highlighting industry best practices through a case study.

Through the Offshore Wind Science, Research and Analysis program, USD 2.5 million will support 12 projects in advancing research that informs the responsible development and operation of offshore wind in Southern New England and the Gulf of Maine. Each project has a direct connection to a Massachusetts-based business or research institution, a Massachusetts-based intern, or both. Collectively, these awards will create at least seven paid internships for students attending Massachusetts universities, giving early-career researchers hands-on experience in offshore wind science.

This year’s awards will address five topic areas: Fisheries; Habitat & Wildlife; Regional Transmission Planning; Regional Monitoring; and Science Communication.

The 2026 Offshore Wind Science, Research and Analysis awardees are:

New England Aquarium: USD 246,075 for Fisheries research

Funding will be used to research how offshore wind development is affecting recreational and for-hire fishing activity in Southern New England.

Partners: Pelagic Strategies

UMass Dartmouth

USD 280,501 for Fisheries and Habitat research

Funding will be used to continue a study focused on understanding offshore wind impacts on cod spawning grounds in Southern New England.

USD 199,589 for Regional Monitoring

Funding will be used to create a regional data-collection strategy to guide future monitoring and inform responsible offshore wind development in the Gulf of Maine.

Partners: Regional Wildlife Science Collaborative & Northeast Regional Ocean Council (separate $30,000 award to support this project)

Center for Coastal Studies: USD 284,642 for Habitat & Wildlife research

Funding will be used to evaluate the ability of ocean circulation models to predict zooplankton aggregations to inform methods for understanding potential offshore wind effects on North Atlantic right whale prey.

Partners: Integral Consulting

atdepth MRV Inc.: USD 252,000 for Habitat & Wildlife research

Funding will be used to create a digital twin model of the Gulf of Maine to study potential effects of floating offshore wind turbines on ocean processes and North Atlantic right whale prey.

Tufts University: USD 269,910 for Habitat & Wildlife research

Funding will be used to develop an implementation framework for incorporating nature-inclusive design into offshore wind projects.

Partners: Outer Harbor Consulting; Responsible Offshore Science Alliance; Nomadic Foundry

JASCO: USD 246,746 for Habitat & Wildlife research

Funding will be used to examine existing offshore wind wildlife protection measures using quantitative modeling to assess risk reduction and implementation costs.

Ocean Tech Services, LLC: USD 77,414 for Habitat & Wildlife research

Funding will be used to install a Motus radio telemetry receiving station at the Woods Hole Oceanographic Institute’s Air-Sea Interaction Tower, re-establishing important offshore detection capability for migratory birds and bats.

Power Advisory LLC: USD 186,995 for Regional Transmission

Funding will be used to build on existing offshore wind energy transmission studies to investigate interregional transmission scenarios for New England, New York, and Atlantic Canada.

Partners: Johns Hopkins University; UMass Amherst

Responsible Offshore Science Alliance: USD 149,997 for Science Communication

Funding will be used to communicate results of existing offshore wind fisheries research to Massachusetts fishing communities and the general public.

Partners: Fat Moon Creative

Biodiversity Research Institute: USD 149,206 for Science Communication

Funding will be used to translate and communicate offshore wind science and research into accessible, stakeholder-informed materials for Massachusetts and beyond.

Partners: Consensus Building Institute

CBN Media, LLC: USD 125,000 for Science Communication

Funding will be used to increase public understanding of marine life interactions with offshore wind infrastructure in Southern New England.

text:
A coalition of 16 state attorneys general is intensifying the political fight over corporate climate transparency, warning that support for climate-related disclosures could expose the Big Four accounting firms to liability under state law.

The letter, led by officials in Florida, Texas, Nebraska, and Alaska, takes aim at Deloitte, EY, PwC, and KPMG, adding uncertainty to efforts meant to help companies, investors, and communities gauge the financial risks of the warming world.

Here's what to know

The publicly released letter argues that support for climate-reporting initiatives may be at odds with accounting firms' obligations to maintain independence, objectivity, and integrity.

According to ESG Today, the attorneys general focused on the firms' involvement with the Task Force on Climate-Related Financial Disclosures, the now-disbanded Net Zero Financial Service Providers Alliance, and their endorsement of the International Sustainability Standards Board's climate-reporting standard.

The states say those commitments could create conflicts of interest if the firms are promoting disclosures that boost demand for their own accounting and auditing work. They also contend that the firms' public statements about independence and integrity may raise concerns under state unfair and deceptive acts and practices laws.

The letter says that any violations could have implications for state and federal contracting, warning that they "could result in penalties and termination of the Big Four's contracts," ESG Today reported.

The attorneys general asked for records and responses concerning their support for climate-reporting efforts and related pledges, including questions about effects on farmers and small businesses in public-company supply chains as well as independence, conflicts, advertising, and disclosure of those commitments.

The letter was also signed by the attorneys general of Alabama, Arkansas, Idaho, Iowa, Mississippi, Montana, North Dakota, Ohio, Oklahoma, South Carolina, South Dakota, and West Virginia.

More background

The letter fits into a Republican-led campaign against climate-related disclosure rules in the United States and abroad.

U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission Chair Paul Atkins has said the agency could reconsider rules allowing foreign issuers to file under International Financial Reporting Standards because the IFRS Foundation backs the ISSB, ESG Today noted.

In the states' view, climate reporting adds costs for farmers and small businesses that are part of public-company supply chains.

What's being done?

Among other things, the letter asks the firms to spell out their ties to climate-reporting initiatives, explain how those commitments square with auditor independence requirements, and describe the potential effects on smaller businesses, according to ESG Today.

Even so, the wider push for disclosure continues. Many companies, regulators, and investors still view climate-risk reporting as a practical way to identify physical and financial vulnerabilities, especially as weather-related disruptions grow more expensive.

"The Big 4's climate commitments force clients to make burdensome climate-related disclosures that drive up the costs of their services and place onerous requirements on farmers and small businesses," Nebraska Attorney General Mike Hilgers said, per ESG Today. "These costs will ultimately be passed onto consumers, who will be forced to bear the burden of increased prices for food, energy, and other everyday products."

Where can I learn more?

This clash over climate transparency stretches well beyond the states' warning to the Big Four. California is pressing ahead with broad disclosure mandates even as federal regulators and Republican-led states try to weaken, block, or roll back similar rules elsewhere.

• California's new corporate disclosure laws could force major companies to reveal climate risks nationwide.

• At the SEC, moves to erase climate reporting rules could leave investors with less clarity.

• In Texas, officials barred a major bank from local contracts over climate commitments.

• In Florida, lawmakers backed deleting climate change references from state law.

The larger tug of war is one reason the pressure campaign directed at Deloitte, EY, PwC, and KPMG bears watching.

text:
People across Wales are being invited to have their say on proposals for a new public energy company owned by the people of Wales.

Proposals for a new public energy company aims to keep the benefits of our abundant energy sources in Wales

It could help bring down energy costs over the longer term.

Energy Minister says: “It’s about cheaper, cleaner energy that is made and owned in Wales.”

A consultation launched today, sets out proposals for a single national public energy company. The company would bring together existing energy organisations and help ensure that more of the economic benefits from Wales’s energy resources flow to people, communities, businesses and public services in Wales.

Wales has some of the best renewable energy resources in Europe. The proposed company would aim to increase Welsh ownership of energy projects and help communities, businesses and public services make better use of energy produced in Wales.

The company would not replace existing energy suppliers or directly set household energy prices. However, increasing Welsh ownership of energy projects could help reduce energy costs over time and ensure more money is reinvested in Welsh communities and public services.

Cabinet Minister for Enterprise, Connectivity and Energy, Adam Price, said: 'Wales has huge potential to generate clean energy from our natural resources. We want to make sure the benefits of that energy are felt by people and communities across Wales, both in jobs and growth but eventually in lower bills too.

'Wales is on the verge of a second (or another) energy revolution and this time we want to make sure we keep more of the benefits here. This consultation is about how we can build a stronger Welsh energy sector, support local ownership and create lasting value for future generations. It’s about cheaper, cleaner energy that is made and owned in Wales. We want to hear from people, communities, businesses and organisations across Wales about how this company should work and what it should deliver.'

While the proposals laid out in this consultation aim to cut energy bills in the future, the Welsh Government is using every tool available to them to help households cope with their energy bills. This year we are investing more than £37 million in our Nest scheme to help low-income families escape cold, damp conditions, and continue to invest in direct support through fuel vouchers and heating assistance.

The Claim What’s Yours service helps people check their eligibility for extra income and guide them through the claiming process. For free, confidential, advice, call 0800 702 2020.

The Nest advice line is open to everyone, offering tips on actions people can take themselves to reduce energy costs as well as assessing eligibility for free energy efficiency measures. Call free on 0808 808 2244.

The consultation is open until 30 November 2026.

text:
In our manifesto we set out the case for a single Welsh Public Energy Company, owned by the people of Wales and working for the people of Wales. Today, I am launching a 12-week public consultation on proposals for the future development of Wales’s public energy functions, including the establishment of this company.

Our ambition is clear. Wales must build more of the clean energy it needs, own more of it, and benefit more directly from it. More clean power, more public consent and more Welsh ownership will mean more economic and social value retained in Wales, supporting a stronger and more prosperous Welsh economy. Wales has made good progress in planning for our clean energy future. We now need to deliver, with a clear focus on decentralisation, matching clean energy generation to Wales’s natural resources and supporting local use.

The consultation seeks views on how we can bring together existing public energy functions into a single Welsh Public Energy Company. The proposed company would help take our existing energy plans through to financed, Welsh-owned, operating projects. It will accelerate delivery, strengthen public sector capability, support community and local ownership, and retain a greater share of the value from the energy transition in Wales.

At a local scale, there are significant opportunities to support communities, co-operatives, local authorities and other public bodies to develop and own renewable energy projects, including onshore wind and solar. The consultation also seeks views on how smarter local energy systems can be accelerated across Wales. This includes exploring models such as homes and buildings acting as power stations, community batteries, local heat networks, mine-water heat, local tariffs, and other approaches that help match local generation with local demand. These approaches can help households, businesses and communities play a more active role in the energy system of the future.

For developments of national significance and scale, such as the major opportunities presented by offshore wind, Wales must be positioned to land clean power, capture value, support our industries and create good Welsh jobs.

This consultation is an important step in moving from ambition to delivery. It will help shape how Wales strengthens its public energy capability, increases Welsh ownership, supports communities, and ensures more of the benefits from the clean energy transition are retained here in Wales.

I encourage individuals, communities, public bodies, businesses and stakeholders across Wales to respond to the consultation and help shape the next stage of Wales’s clean energy future.

The consultation will close on 30 November 2026.

This statement is being issued during recess to keep Members informed. Should Members wish me to make a further statement or to answer questions on this when the Senedd returns I would be happy to do so.

text:
The new-generation Li Mega and upcoming Li i9 will gradually switch from CATL batteries to batteries developed in-house by Li Auto.

Pre-orders for the 2026 Li i6 will open in late September, with deliveries starting in early November.

Li Auto (NASDAQ: LI) plans to roll out batteries developed in-house across its entire lineup and launch the 2026 Li i6 electric SUV (sport utility vehicle) with its own battery and chip in the fourth quarter.

The Chinese automaker detailed the roll-out in a WeChat post on Monday, advancing its strategy to control core battery and chip technologies.

The 2026 Li i6 will feature Li Auto's in-house 5C battery and Mach assisted-driving chip. Pre-orders will open in late September, with deliveries starting in early November.

The Li i6, a 5-seat all-electric SUV, was first launched in September 2025. The updated model will bring more internally developed core components to one of the company's key products.

Li i6 deliveries totaled 135,863 in the first 7 months of this year, according to data compiled by CnEVPost. July deliveries fell 28.12% from June to 15,420, but still accounted for about half of the company's monthly total.

Li Auto said its in-house batteries are already used in the Li L8, Li L6 and Li i8, with deployment set to expand to all models.

Initial deliveries of the new-generation Li Mega use 5C ternary lithium batteries from CATL (HKEX: 3750). The model will switch entirely to Li Auto's in-house 5C ternary lithium batteries once production preparations are complete.

Orders in the first few days after the new-generation Li Mega's launch exceeded expectations, leaving CATL battery inventories close to depletion, the company said.

Customers who lock in Li Mega orders at or after 3:00 pm Beijing Time on September 7 will receive vehicles with Li Auto's in-house batteries. Deliveries are expected to begin in November.

Li Auto launched the new-generation Li Mega on September 2, pairing a lower price with major hardware upgrades to boost demand for the flagship all-electric MPV (multi-purpose vehicle). Initial deliveries began on September 5.

The Li i9, a flagship 6-seat all-electric SUV set to debut in mid-September, will also initially use CATL's 5C ternary lithium batteries.

The Li i9 will switch entirely to Li Auto's in-house batteries once production ramps up.

Li Auto began developing battery cells in-house in 2020, with its technology now covering 5C cells, battery packs and the battery management system (BMS), it said.

The company said integrated battery and vehicle design, along with its experience in 5C ultra-fast charging, would support battery quality, safety and long-life.

Development of the Mach chip began in 2022, and Li Auto plans to continue investing in future iterations.

The technology shift comes as Li Auto increases its investment in a battery manufacturing partner. Sunwoda (SZSE: 300207) disclosed on September 4 that Li Auto plans to inject capital into its power battery subsidiary, Sunwoda Electric Vehicle Battery Co Ltd (Sunwoda EVB).

Li Auto will directly hold an 8.79% stake in Sunwoda EVB after the transaction, becoming its second-largest single shareholder.

The companies established a 50-50 joint venture in 2025 to manufacture batteries developed by Li Auto.

Scaling up the use of internally developed components is also a key part of Li Auto's response to cost pressures. Its vehicle margin was 9.4% in the second quarter, down from 19.4% a year earlier.

Management said on an August 26 earnings call that it would control costs through integrated design, in-house technology and supply chain optimization, and had decided against passing the latest cost increases on to customers.

FADA President Sai Giridhar identified the historic shift in passenger vehicle powertrains as the defining element of the performance.

text:
New Delhi [India], September 7 (ANI): Indian automobile retail recorded its biggest-ever August as alternative fuels overtook petrol in the passenger vehicle segment for the first time in history, according to the Federation of Automobile Dealers Associations (FADA).

Total vehicle retail registrations reached 24,23,201 units in August 2026, marking a 17.51 per cent increase compared to the corresponding period last year. Retails, however, slipped 6.48 per cent month-on-month due to seasonal monsoon patterns and calendar shifts that moved festival buying into September.

FADA President Sai Giridhar identified the historic shift in passenger vehicle powertrains as the defining element of the performance.

'The defining development of the month, however, was a structural one: for the first time in India's history, alternative fuels - CNG, hybrid and electric combined - overtook petrol in the Passenger Vehicle market, at 41.95% against petrol's 40.85%,' Giridhar said.

'A little over a year ago petrol led this contest by nearly eleven percentage points; that lead has now been erased,' he added.

Segment details show CNG captured 25.28 per cent, hybrids secured 9.04 per cent, and electric vehicles accounted for 7.63 per cent of the passenger vehicle market. Dealers noted that running costs and buyer hesitation regarding the E20 transition directed demand toward alternative fuel options, even as petrol remained the largest standalone fuel category.

Total passenger vehicle retail reached 4,02,398 units, registering a 16.14 per cent growth year-on-year to cross the four-lakh milestone for any August.

text:
China has temporarily paused approvals for new battery manufacturing projects for energy storage as authorities review existing and planned production capacity amid concerns over overcapacity, according to a report by Chinese financial news outlet Cailianshe.

The review is focused particularly on battery cells, with authorities assessing the scale of capacity already in place and projects in the pipeline, Cailianshe reported, citing people in the industry.

Projects that have not yet started construction will be put on hold for now, while those already under construction will not be affected, according to the report. The policy could be adjusted later depending on market conditions.

The move does not amount to a blanket halt on China's energy storage industry. Instead, it signals a more cautious approach towards adding new production capacity at a time when manufacturers are facing intensifying competition and pressure on prices.

Why China is reviewing battery capacity

China has rapidly expanded its energy storage manufacturing base alongside its large-scale deployment of renewable energy. Batteries are increasingly being used to store electricity from intermittent sources such as solar and wind, balance power grids and provide backup power.

Demand for energy storage batteries has continued to grow, but manufacturers have also been grappling with excess capacity. Intense competition has contributed to falling prices and pressure on profit margins.

The problems mirror those seen in other Chinese industries, including solar panels and electric vehicles, where rapid investment and aggressive capacity expansion have led to intense price competition.

China's solar manufacturers have also moved into battery energy storage as a way to diversify beyond solar panels, where overcapacity and weak profitability have weighed on the industry.

Beijing moves to rationalise capacity

The latest move is part of broader efforts by Chinese authorities to address excess capacity in new-energy industries.

China has already taken measures affecting the battery and solar sectors. In July, the country introduced a consumption tax on lithium-ion batteries and solar cells as part of efforts to rationalise the industries.

The temporary pause could therefore give authorities time to assess whether planned energy storage investments match expected demand rather than allowing production capacity to expand unchecked.

At the same time, the underlying demand outlook for energy storage remains strong. The growth of renewable power generation and the need for grid flexibility are expected to increase demand for batteries capable of storing electricity and supplying it when needed.

The distinction between existing projects and new projects is significant. Facilities already under construction are not affected by the reported pause, meaning China's current manufacturing expansion will continue even as authorities reassess future capacity additions.

The latest development also highlights a broader challenge for China's clean-energy industries: maintaining its manufacturing advantage while preventing excess capacity, falling prices and weak returns from undermining the sector.

For global energy markets, any sustained tightening of new battery manufacturing capacity in China could eventually affect the supply outlook for energy storage systems, although the immediate impact is expected to be limited because projects already under construction can continue.

Subheading: The Electric Vehicle Association of the Philippines is urging the government to extend the country's zero-import-tariff policy for electric vehicles until 2040, arguing that longer-term incentives could accelerate EV adoption and support the development of the domestic electric mobility industry.

MANILA, Philippines – September 7, 2026: The Electric Vehicle Association of the Philippines (EVAP) is pushing for the Philippines to extend its zero-tariff policy on electric vehicles until 2040, as the industry seeks longer-term policy support to accelerate EV adoption and strengthen the country's electric mobility ecosystem.

EVAP Vice President Carla Buencamino said the industry group wants the existing zero-tariff policy to continue beyond its current expiration in 2028. She described an extension through 2040 as an ideal scenario that could provide greater certainty for the country's growing EV industry.

The proposal comes as the Philippines works toward ambitious electric vehicle adoption targets and expands its charging infrastructure. The government currently has a target of achieving 50 percent EV penetration by 2040 and 60 percent by 2050.

Philippines Currently Has Zero Tariffs on Several EV Categories

The Philippine government has removed import tariffs on several categories of electric and electrified vehicles, including battery electric vehicles (BEVs), hybrid electric vehicles (HEVs), plug-in hybrid electric vehicles (PHEVs) and certain EV parts and components.

However, the current zero-tariff policy is scheduled to remain in place only until 2028. EVAP is now calling for the incentive to be extended through 2040 to provide longer-term support for EV adoption and industry development.

According to EVAP, maintaining or improving incentives will be important as the Philippines attempts to increase the share of electric vehicles on its roads and build a stronger domestic EV ecosystem.

Why EVAP Wants the Policy Extended Until 2040

The EV industry association believes that long-term policy support can give automakers, importers, charging companies and other businesses greater certainty when making investments in the Philippine EV market.

A longer zero-tariff period could also help keep EV prices more competitive by reducing the import-duty burden on eligible vehicles and components. This could potentially make electric mobility more accessible to consumers while encouraging companies to expand their presence in the country.

EVAP Vice President Carla Buencamino said the industry needs incentives to be sustained, if not further improved, to encourage continued EV adoption and support the sector's growth.

Philippines Targets 50% EV Penetration by 2040

The push for a longer zero-tariff policy comes as the Philippine government works toward significant electrification targets.

The current government target calls for EVs to account for 50 percent of vehicles by 2040 and 60 percent by 2050.

Energy Secretary Sharon Garin has also indicated that the government is considering raising those ambitions, with EVs potentially accounting for 60 percent of the country's vehicles by 2040 and 80 percent by 2050.

Achieving these targets would require continued investment across the EV ecosystem, including vehicles, charging infrastructure, energy systems, manufacturing and supporting services.

Senate Bill 2270 Seeks Longer EV Incentives

The EVAP proposal is also supported by legislative efforts to strengthen and extend incentives for the electric vehicle industry.

In June, Senator Sherwin Gatchalian filed Senate Bill 2270, which seeks to amend the Electric Vehicle Industry Development Act, or Republic Act 11697.

The proposed legislation would extend the validity of fiscal and non-fiscal EV incentives from eight years to 12 years. It also proposes a zero-percent import duty on electric vehicles, as well as related equipment and infrastructure.

The bill additionally proposes several non-fiscal incentives for EV users, including:

Waived or discounted parking fees for eligible EV users.

Toll-free access to dedicated EV expressway lanes.

A Buy Now, Register Later program.

EVAP has expressed support for these initiatives, saying continued government assistance will be important for sustaining the country's transition toward electric mobility.

Government Procurement Could Drive EV Adoption

EVAP is also calling for the Philippine government to take a stronger leadership role in EV adoption through its own vehicle procurement programs.

Government agencies represent a significant potential fleet market. Greater adoption of EVs in government fleets could increase demand for electric vehicles while providing a visible example of the technology's suitability for everyday transportation.

During his 2026 State of the Nation Address, President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. said the government had been directed to prioritize electric vehicles in its vehicle re-fleeting plans.

EVAP believes continued government support, combined with private-sector adoption, could help accelerate the country's transition toward electric mobility.

Charging Infrastructure Remains Critical

Extending EV incentives alone will not be enough to achieve large-scale EV adoption. Charging infrastructure will also need to expand significantly as the number of electric vehicles on Philippine roads increases.

EVAP has called for government processes related to charging infrastructure to be streamlined to facilitate faster deployment.

ACMobility, one of the companies involved in the country's EV charging ecosystem, is targeting more than 1,000 EV charging points within 2026.

The company has already deployed more than 500 charging points across more than 230 locations nationwide, according to the report. Around 70 percent of its charging points are located in the Greater Metro Manila area.

ACMobility Expands EV Charging and Safety Initiatives

Through its EV charging solutions arm Greenstrum, ACMobility is also supporting businesses that want to establish their own EV charging capabilities as electric vehicle usage increases.

The company has additionally launched an EV Safety Program designed to address common misconceptions about electric vehicles and provide consumers with practical information about EV safety and operation.

ACMobility CEO Jaime Alfonso Zobel de Ayala said the company's objective is to help build an end-to-end electric mobility ecosystem while giving Filipino drivers the information and tools needed to make the transition to electric transportation.

Long-Term Policy Could Shape the Philippine EV Market

The proposed extension of zero tariffs highlights the importance of policy continuity in developing an emerging EV market.

Electric vehicle adoption depends on several interconnected factors, including vehicle prices, charging availability, consumer awareness, financing, government incentives and the availability of suitable EV models.

A long-term tariff policy could provide manufacturers and other industry participants with greater visibility when planning investments, while potentially helping consumers access a wider range of electric vehicles at more competitive prices.

At the same time, the Philippines will need to balance import incentives with its longer-term objective of developing domestic capabilities across the EV value chain, including vehicle assembly, battery manufacturing, components and charging infrastructure.

What Happens Next?

For now, the extension of the zero-tariff policy until 2040 remains an industry proposal rather than an approved policy change. The existing zero-tariff measures are scheduled to continue until 2028.

EVAP's push, together with Senate Bill 2270 and the government's stated EV adoption targets, could lead to further discussions about the country's long-term electric mobility policy.

The outcome will be closely watched by automakers, EV distributors, charging companies, fleet operators and consumers as the Philippines works to increase electric vehicle adoption over the coming decade.

Conclusion

The Electric Vehicle Association of the Philippines is calling for the country's zero-import-tariff policy on electric vehicles to be extended from its current 2028 deadline through 2040.

The proposal comes as the Philippines targets a 50 percent EV penetration rate by 2040 and considers even more ambitious electrification goals. Alongside longer-term incentives, the country will need continued investment in charging infrastructure, government fleet electrification and the broader EV supply chain.

Whether the zero-tariff policy is extended will be an important factor in determining the pace and direction of the Philippine EV market as the country moves toward its 2040 electrification targets.

Frequently Asked Questions

Does the Philippines currently have zero tariffs on EVs?

Yes. The Philippine government has removed tariffs on battery electric vehicles, hybrid electric vehicles, plug-in hybrid electric vehicles and certain EV parts and components, with the current policy scheduled to remain in effect until 2028.

Is the Philippines extending the EV zero-tariff policy until 2040?

Not yet. The Electric Vehicle Association of the Philippines is lobbying for the policy to be extended until 2040, but the proposed extension has not been presented as an approved government policy.

Why does EVAP want zero tariffs until 2040?

EVAP believes longer-term incentives would help encourage EV adoption, provide greater policy certainty for businesses and support continued growth of the Philippine electric mobility industry.

What is the Philippines' EV adoption target?

The current government target is for EVs to account for 50 percent of vehicles by 2040 and 60 percent by 2050. Government officials have also discussed potentially raising these targets.

What is Senate Bill 2270?

Senate Bill 2270 seeks to amend the Electric Vehicle Industry Development Act by extending fiscal and non-fiscal incentives from eight to 12 years and introducing zero-percent import duty on EVs, related equipment and infrastructure.

How important is charging infrastructure for EV adoption in the Philippines?

Charging infrastructure is a critical part of EV adoption. Industry representatives have called for streamlined government processes to accelerate charging-point deployment across the country.

text:
Arthur Yuen, Deputy Chief Executive of the Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA), announced the official launch of the Phase 2B prototype of the Hong Kong Sustainable Finance Taxonomy in conjunction with the opening of Hong Kong Green Week 2026, along with a one-month public consultation. The new phase expands the total number of economic activities from 25 to 39, incorporating transition activities such as steel manufacturing, battery recycling, and electric buses for the first time, while also introducing a process-based climate adaptation assessment framework to further strengthen Hong Kong's sustainable finance infrastructure.

In an article published on the HKMA's "InSight" column, Yuen noted that the continuous development and optimization of the taxonomy aims to establish a clear and credible assessment tool for the market, clearly defining which economic activities contribute to green and sustainable development, enabling investment and financing decisions to be evidence-based and facilitating the flow of related capital. He revealed that many banks and corporations have already applied the taxonomy to their investment, financing activities, and sustainable finance frameworks, boosting investor confidence in the "green credentials" of projects.

The funding for Hong Kong's first public hydrogen refueling station came from a green loan certified as compliant with the taxonomy standards. The market has also launched multiple bonds and loans that meet taxonomy standards, covering sectors such as transportation and energy. Kenneth Chan, Executive Director at the HKMA, added that financing models applying the taxonomy include loans and bond issuance, with amounts ranging from tens of millions to billions of Hong Kong dollars, primarily related to energy efficiency and renewable energy projects.

Climate Change Mitigation: 10 New Activities Targeting Hard-to-Abate Sectors

Phase 2B continues to focus on the two major objectives of "mitigation" and "adaptation" to climate change. On the mitigation front, 10 new economic activities have been added across three sectors—transportation, manufacturing, and waste treatment—with three key priorities: supporting critical technologies to drive emissions reduction, providing transition pathways for "hard-to-abate sectors," and facilitating the development of green transportation and low-carbon fuels.

The new phase adds activities including battery manufacturing, battery recycling, and low-carbon technology manufacturing. For steel manufacturing, the authority has established two assessment pathways: one based on "emissions intensity" that recognizes incremental emissions reduction achievements, and another based on "technology improvement" that encourages the adoption of advanced emissions reduction technologies. Companies can select the appropriate assessment approach based on their circumstances, advancing their decarbonization transition within a pragmatic and feasible framework.

On electrification, Phase 2B covers economic activities related to the procurement and use of electric buses, electric minibuses, and electric taxis, supporting the reduction of conventional fuel usage. On low-carbon fuels, the new phase covers the entire Sustainable Aviation Fuel (SAF) value chain, including production, blending, storage, and application, as well as green marine fuels such as the production and application of methanol and ammonia.

Climate Adaptation: First-Ever Process-Based Assessment Approach

Unlike climate "mitigation," climate "adaptation" requires consideration of geographical factors. Even when facing the same risks, different locations may require entirely different response measures. Accordingly, Phase 2B introduces a Process-based Approach (PBA)—a systematic "five-step method" that provides clear guidance on defining project scope, risk identification, measure design and implementation, ongoing monitoring, and continuous improvement.

The PBA retains flexibility to accommodate different scenarios while maintaining rigorous and consistent assessment principles. The approach emphasizes ease of market application: if project proponents have already updated design standards or undertaken other relevant work in response to climate change, certain assessment steps may be simplified or skipped as appropriate to avoid duplicate evaluation.

On climate "adaptation," Phase 2B introduces two categories of measures: "whitelist" and "non-whitelist." Whitelist measures have undergone rigorous assessment and are confirmed to make substantive contributions to climate adaptation. The new phase adds 11 whitelist measures, expanding coverage to the energy, transportation, construction, information and communications technology, and risk management and response sectors.

Non-whitelist measures focus on coastal management and flood management, referencing the Hong Kong SAR Government's guidelines to provide a reference list in the taxonomy, identifying 13 non-whitelist measures and examples of technical indicators used for assessment.

Green Finance Market Performance and Future Plans

Hong Kong is a leading green and sustainable bond issuance platform in Asia. In the first half of this year, green and sustainable bonds issued in Hong Kong totaled $20.2 billion (approximately NT$640 billion), up 3% year-on-year, outperforming the region's flat growth.

Chan expects the Phase 2B taxonomy to be officially launched between the end of this year and early next year, with systematic data collection on bank usage to begin in the second half of next year. The HKMA will further expand the scope of the taxonomy in the future. The HKMA previously launched the first phase and Phase 2A of the taxonomy in May 2024 and January of this year, respectively.

Yuen stated that the HKMA will continue to leverage Green Week to consolidate and enhance Hong Kong's influence as a sustainable finance hub. The authority will also develop practical application guidelines based on market needs, assist the industry in effectively utilizing the taxonomy, and gather insights on banking sector adoption through surveys and other means, providing reference for future discussions on whether to incorporate the taxonomy into banking supervisory policy.

The third Hong Kong Green Week is being held this week, attracting over 100 local and international public and private sector organizations, with approximately 60 events scheduled. The HKMA will continue to be guided by market developments, public policy, industry priorities, and the latest technological advancements in updating the taxonomy, while maintaining communication with market participants and stakeholders to drive the taxonomy's greater role in Hong Kong's sustainable finance ecosystem.

title: High Fuel Prices Are Powering an Electric Motorcycle Boom | OilPrice.com
description:
Two-wheel vehicles have long been popular in busy cities and low-income countries, and now, largely due to rising fuel prices, many are investing in electric two-wheelers.
While the electric version of these vehicles is generally more expensive than petrol-powered ones, they can be cheaper and more reliable to run in the long term, given the volatility of fossil fuel prices.
In addition to the rise in oil prices, which has driven demand, government subsidies have also supported the trend.
The Chinese electric bike maker TAILG partnered with Ghanaian battery-swapping operator Kofa to develop the TK90 electric motorcycle, which is tailored exclusively for the African market.
In addition to their rising popularity in low-income countries, e-motorcycles are also gaining traction in certain market segments in other parts of the world.
text:
While electric car and truck sales have grown more slowly than expected in recent years, prompting governments to rethink clean fuel targets and automakers to slow the pace of EV production, electric motorcycles are becoming increasingly popular in certain parts of the world. Two-wheel vehicles have long been popular in busy cities and low-income countries, and now, largely due to rising fuel prices, many are investing in electric two-wheelers.

The United States-Israeli attacks on Iran in February, which led to the ongoing Iran War and spurred the closure of the Strait of Hormuz, have driven oil and gas prices up sharply in recent months. Many countries have faced energy shortages, and everyone has been forced to pay a premium to access much-needed fuel. This has hit some regions of the world harder than others, disproportionately affecting low-income countries.

Some of the most affected markets, such as those in Southeast Asia and Africa, have long used motorcycles as a low-cost means of navigating crowded cities. While the electric version of these vehicles is generally more expensive than petrol-powered ones, they can be cheaper and more reliable to run in the long term, given the volatility of fossil fuel prices. As it is often cheaper now to charge a battery than to fill a fuel tank, many people are making the switch.

In Pakistan, motorbikes make up about 80 per cent of vehicles on the road. E-motorcycles were rarely seen just a few years ago, but the trend has grown in popularity, with new brands entering the market every week. Models from around 84 companies are now available in Pakistan. The rise in popularity has given way to small startups, backed by venture capital, as well as traditional electric vehicle (EV) makers.

The sale of electric two-wheelers rose by 173 per cent in Pakistan in the first half of the year, according to market-intelligence firm Motorcycles Data. In addition to the rise in oil prices, which has driven demand, government subsidies have also supported the trend. Many of the motorcycles being sold in Pakistan come from China, although some companies are fitting domestically produced motorbikes with Chinese motors.

In Vietnam, where motorcycles have long been popular due to heavy congestion, automakers are seeing electric two-wheeler sales soar. The establishment of a low-emission zone in Hanoi’s city centre, which restricts the use of gasoline-powered motorcycles on weekends, is driving uptake in the capital. Vietnam’s VinFast saw record e-motorcycle order volumes in the first quarter of 2026. VinFast delivered 143,136 electric motorbikes and e-bikes in the first three months of the year, up by 219 per cent from the same period in 2025.

In July, Japan’s Honda Motor announced plans to begin production of its UC3 electric motorcycle in Vietnam starting this year. Honda is expected to develop production facilities in the northern province of Phu Tho. Honda’s Vietnam’s general director, Sayaka Arai, stated, “The trend toward electrification among consumers is moving forward more than expected.” She added that higher fuel prices, driven by the ongoing war in Iran, have further accelerated consumer interest in electric scooters and motorcycles.

The wider availability of more affordable Chinese EVs has driven uptake in recent years. More Chinese brands have opened stores selling e-motorcycles and other EVs across Asia and Africa, helping to drive up sales. Some Chinese companies have partnered with local firms to adapt their EVs for the local market to further boost demand.

The Chinese electric bike maker TAILG partnered with Ghanaian battery-swapping operator Kofa to develop the TK90 electric motorcycle, which is tailored exclusively for the African market. The duo created the TK90 with a swappable lithium battery and reduced the motorcycle’s operating costs by around 30 per cent. The model is now available in Kenya and Tanzania.

TAILG is also developing a solar-powered three-wheeler with over 25 per cent power generation efficiency. It is currently testing solar panels on outdoor battery swap cabinets across Africa. The rollout of these units could enable consumers to use an e-motorcycle in regions not yet equipped with sufficient charging infrastructure. The lack of charging points has been a major bottleneck to EV uptake in some countries, such as Kenya, where consumers have been deterred from investing in e-motorcycles for fear they cannot charge them in many areas.

In addition to their rising popularity in low-income countries, e-motorcycles are also gaining traction in certain market segments in other parts of the world. In California, e-motorcycles, e-scooters, and e-mopeds have become more popular among teenagers seeking access to cleaner, low-cost transportation. Sales have been steadily growing since the Covid-19 pandemic.

The sale of e-motorcycles is expected to continue to rise as a broader range of models becomes available, and consumers increasingly look to switch to cleaner modes of transportation. The trend is also being driven by the volatility in oil and gas prices, with the ongoing conflict in the Middle East demonstrating how an overreliance on fossil fuels can threaten energy security.

name: North Carolina Environment
title: Carbon credit financing emerges as Africa's biggest bet for expanding clean cooking
description:
Africa is moving faster to adopt clean cookstoves In June, the IEA announced Africa had secured $900 million in new financial commitments towards clean cooking technologies.
More than 30 governments in countries accounting for about 80% of Africans who still lack access to clean cooking have introduced 121 new clean cooking policies since the Paris climate summit in 2015, the energy agency said.
Clean cooking is not a luxury, but an everyday necessity affecting every household, Tanzanian President Samia Suluhu said after co-hosting an IEA conference on clean cooking in Dar es Salaam earlier this year.
Critics of the approach say relying too heavily on carbon credits to finance clean cooking is still risky.
Clean cooking is expanding despite the shortcomings Companies are adapting their approach to suit local conditions.
text:
NAIROBI, Kenya (AP) — Every morning, Mary Kavutha prepares breakfast for her two young children using an induction cooker in her Nairobi home. Two years ago, the businesswoman relied on a charcoal stove that filled her kitchen with smoke and cost about $1.15 in fuel each day.

Today, she says, for 80 cents in electricity tokens she can cook several meals.

“It cooks much faster, and is much safer because I have young children,” Kavutha said. “With charcoal there was always smoke in the house. Now I can cook indoors comfortably, and I spend much less.”

Nearly 1 billion Africans still rely on charcoal or firewood for everyday cooking. The International Energy Agency (IEA) estimates that household air pollution from these fuels contributes to about 850,000 deaths annually on the continent.

Like millions of other Africans, Kavutha switched not out of climate concerns but because the stoves are affordable since they are underwritten by carbon credit financing, which allows clean cooking companies to raise capital against future revenues from emission reductions.

Clean cooking companies are betting that carbon finance, long criticized over concerns about the credibility of some projects, could become Africa's most important tool for expanding cleaner household energy and reducing pressure on forests.

Africa is moving faster to adopt clean cookstoves

In June, the IEA announced Africa had secured $900 million in new financial commitments towards clean cooking technologies.

More than 30 governments in countries accounting for about 80% of Africans who still lack access to clean cooking have introduced 121 new clean cooking policies since the Paris climate summit in 2015, the energy agency said.

Clean cooking is not a luxury, but an everyday necessity affecting every household, Tanzanian President Samia Suluhu said after co-hosting an IEA conference on clean cooking in Dar es Salaam earlier this year. That followed the African Union’s Dar es Salaam Declaration on Clean Cooking, adopted by 30 governments last year.

Carbon financing is making clean cooking affordable

Carbon finance has transformed what was once an expensive clean-energy product into one that millions of low-income households can afford, said Peter Scott, founder and CEO of BURN, which makes eco-friendly cookstoves.

“The only way clean cooking is going to scale on the continent is through carbon project finance,” Scott said. “Governments earn revenue and customers get a product they would never have been able to afford without that subsidy.”

The Nairobi-based firm said it has distributed more than 7.3 million cookstoves in 11 African countries.

“Our biggest innovation is not the stove itself, but the financing behind it,” Scott said. “Without that financing, many families cannot afford to switch.”

An efficient biomass stove that would normally retail for about $40 can cost customers as little as $5 after carbon subsidies. More expensive induction cookers are financed through carbon credits and short-term pay-as-you-go plans that spread payments over several months.

“Investors provide upfront capital that subsidizes the retail price of our stoves. In return, they receive revenue from carbon credits generated as households reduce their use of charcoal, wood and other polluting fuels,” he said.

Credit markets are still under scrutiny

The industry has adopted strict standards and more sophisticated measuring of emissions, including Bluetooth monitoring, digital verification and real-time usage data to address criticism of carbon credits.

Critics of the approach say relying too heavily on carbon credits to finance clean cooking is still risky.

In one setback, the Kenyan clean cooking firm Koko Networks, hailed as a poster child of Africa’s green transition, closed in February after failing to win a government letter of authorization to sell carbon credits.

Carbon money can help but should not be the foundation of the transition, said George Mwaniki, WRI Kenya representative and head of Air Quality for WRI Africa.

The problem, he said, is that carbon finance generally comes after the investment required to put cleaner cooking equipment into households.

“Carbon financing is more of a second financing source,” Mwaniki said. “That creates a problem for clean-cooking companies as they need money to manufacture and distribute equipment before they can generate the emissions reductions that ultimately produce carbon credits.”

“If we depend wholly on carbon credits to support the transition, it will be extremely slow and will not happen at the pace that we need it to,” he said.

Clean cooking is expanding despite the shortcomings

Companies are adapting their approach to suit local conditions. BURN, for example, says its electric cooking is more viable in Kenya and Tanzania, while biomass stoves are preferred in the Democratic Republic of Congo and Madagascar.

Eco Safi, which operates in Uganda, Kenya, and Malawi, offers forced-draft pellet stoves and clean, renewable fuel made from agricultural waste. In Rwanda, BioMassters produces smokeless, locally manufactured, solar-powered pellet stoves and biomass-residue fuel, while ENEDOM manufactures agricultural-residue briquettes in Kigali.

For households like Kavutha’s, what matters is that a cleaner stove now costs less to own and operate than the charcoal she once depended on.

“My kitchen is cleaner, my children are safer, and I spend less," Kavutha said. "That is all that matters."

text:
In the US, the push is on to “drill, baby, drill”. In China, the national strategy is to “walk towards the light”. Two energy behemoths, two contrasting approaches to energy.

“Africa’s solar revolution is here,” said Sonia Dunlop, CEO of the Global Solar Council (GSC). “Growth is spreading to new markets across the continent, and rooftop and distributed systems are putting power directly into the hands of households and businesses.”

Wars in Ukraine and the Middle East had delivered “two major fossil fuel supply shocks in four years” that “exposed the brutal cost of energy dependence”, Dunlop noted.
